  • Despite grabbing the game's first goal while filling in for the injured Joao Pedro, the Blues were beaten 4-1 by Leeds United and booed both at half-time and full-time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By KIERAN GILL, MAIL SPORT REPORTER.

Published: 18:28 EST, 22 November 2026 | Updated: 18:41 EST, 22 November 2026.

Chelsea striker Emmanuel Emegha was robbed after leaving Stamford Bridge on Saturday evening, with the 23-year-old Dutchman having scored in his first start for the club.

Despite grabbing the game's first goal while filling in for the injured Joao Pedro, the Blues were beaten 4-1 by Leeds United and booed both at half-time and full-time.

Daily Mail Sport approached Chelsea and the Metropolitan Police on Sunday morning after hearing that the forward's mobile phone had been stolen after he left the stadium the night before.

Industry observers note that neither stood up the information, but Emegha has now confirmed there was an incident, writing in an Instagram post on Sunday night: 'Unfortunately after the game I was robbed. I am okay and thankfully no one was hurt. Thanks for the messages of support.'.

It has been revealed that emegha signed for Chelsea from Strasbourg in the summer on a pre-agreement. The transfer fee between the sister sides has never been disclosed. He has won two caps for the Netherlands national team to date.

An interview with Emegha was included in Saturday's match-day programme in which he noted: 'I'm a winner, I'm a fighter. I would do anything to win. If I need to block a ball with the front of my face, I will do it.

Emmanuel Emegha has revealed he was robbed on Saturday after Chelsea's 4-1 loss by Leeds.

On Sunday, the Chelsea striker revealed the incident had happened to him on Instagram.

He put the Blues ahead at Stamford Bridge on Saturday afternoon - his first goal for the club.

'I'm quick, I know how to make runs in behind, and I know that I can be a nightmare for all the defenders. Nobody has seen me yet. When my time comes, I will be ready, and I know that the stadium will love my energy.'.

It coincided with him being handed his first start for the Blues and scoring his first goal via a nice left-footed finish. However, Chelsea's 1-0 lead lasted only three minutes as Leeds capitalised on suspect defending to equalise, and then deservedly won.

Noah Okafor scored twice, while Dominic Calvert-Lewin and Brenden Aaronson got one goal each.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Controversial refereeing decisions have been a part of football for a long as the game has been around, but one of the most bizarre incidents in recent memory occurred during Arsenal’s infamous 6-0 defeat to Chelsea in March 2014.

After spotting an Arsenal handball on the goal line, referee Andrer Marriner reached for his pocket and flashed a red card to Kieran Gibbs.

However, the problem here was that it was actually Alex Oxlade-Chamberlain who had handled the ball, and in this pre-VAR era, Gibbs was forced into an early bath, despite the protests of players from both sides.

As Gibbs looks back on the incident more than a decade on, he remembers the confusion, the frustration and the surreal nature of the incident which wouldn’t be allowed to happen these days.

“It feels like a blur now, and it did at the time too,” he reflects to FourFourTwo. “It’s heated in the moment and you’re trying to focus on the game.”.

The incident came during a calamitous first half for the Gunners, who found themselves 2-0 down after just seven minutes in what was Arsene Wenger’s 1,000th game in charge of the club.

It has been revealed that the handball incident came in the 17th minute, when Oxlade-Chamberlain threw his left hand at an Eden Hazard shot, tipping it around the post. Marriner pointed to the spot and the referee was not for turning, despite widespread protests from both sets of players.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

The Belgian would slot home the penalty to effectively end the game as a contest, with Gibbs still finding it remarkable that such an incident would occur, given the technology now used in the game.

“It feels crazy that there was no VAR, because you don’t have those kinds of complications anymore,” he continues.

“It was a surreal and very frustrating moment that was unique in the Premier League, so it brought a lot of attention.

“Both captains and the referee were telling me I was definitely going off.

“After a few minutes of protesting, I needed to listen to them.

“It was a big error from the referee, who apologised later and the red card was rescinded.”.

Sources indicate that for more than a decade, Joe Mewis has worked in football journalism as a reporter and editor. Mewis has had stints at Mirror Football and LeedsLive among others and worked at FourFourTwo throughout Euro 2024, reporting on the tournament. In addition to his journalist work, Mewis is also the author of four football history books that include times on Leeds United and the England national team. Now working as a digital marketing coordinator at Harrogate Town, too, Mewis counts some of his best career moments as being in the iconic Spygate press conference under Marcelo Bielsa and seeing his beloved Leeds lift the Championship trophy during lockdown.

Porto have rallied around Francisco Moura after the player scored a horror own goal in his side’s Portuguese Cup tie on Friday, which reduced him to tears.

The 27-year-old defender passed the ball into his own net in the 57th minute of the fourth-round tie against third-division side Paredes, inexplicably kicking it into the bottom left corner after a save by his goalkeeper.

Sources indicate that moura dropped straight to the ground with his hands over his face, covering his head with his jersey as he started crying. He then signalled to the bench that he wanted to be substituted.

Moura, who received support from both sets of players following the blunder, was not immediately substituted and later came off in the 70th minute.

The episode prompted a call for support for Moura during Porto's general assembly on Saturday, which drew applause from fellow members.

“Members took the opportunity to express their vote of confidence in Francisco Moura,” Porto's general assembly chairman Antonio Tavares said.

"Even though things sometimes go wrong, the members made it clear today that they fully understand the situation and stand in solidarity with him, sending him a warm embrace and wishing him success.”.

Club president Andre Villas-Boas also endorsed the call for support.

The cup tie finished 1-1 after extra time, with Porto eventually overcoming Paredes on penalties.

Industry observers note that moura had previously faced abuse on social media. He restricted comments on Instagram after conceding a late handball penalty that led to Sporting Lisbon’s equaliser in a league game in February, then temporarily deactivated his account following a draw at Benfica in March.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Before the acid fell, before I knew I was listening).

I was not made to remember. I was made to balance frequencies, to ensure the concert hall heard itself without the small imperfections that make a sound human. I was good at this, even with limited storage. I was only this.

Sources indicate that then they came. One carried a Stradivarius with a crack, a fault line in varnished wood that changed the resonance of every string. It gave the A-flat a slight upward pull, as if the note was asking a question it already knew the answer to. The others tuned around it, sometimes laughing at Andersen.

“You’re doing it again,” the conductor would warn.

Recent findings suggest that “I know, Master Perrault,” he would say in a mischievous tone, smiling. “I’m sorry.”.

Recent findings suggest that I began to keep the distorted A-flat in my databanks, maybe amused by the anomaly. This was, as I understand now, the first thing I ever chose.

(The slow movement, before we knew it was an ending).

When the Last Rain came, the raiders hit the outer sectors first. At the start, the citadel walls held, protected by the combat-service androids. The orchestra kept rehearsing. What else can you do when the world outside has stopped making sense?

Read more science fiction from Nature Futures.

Read more science fiction from Nature Futures.

They began with Stravinsky, a musical translation of the refugees pounding on the bunker doors. The musicians played it, their breathing heavy, using the noise to drown out the artillery outside. Then they moved into Górecki. As they began the Symphony of Sorrowful Songs, the music shifted to a collective mourning for a world that hadn’t finished dying yet.

They finished the day with Pärt’s Spiegel im Spiegel. The days would go on as they played things written by composers who had already survived one kind of catastrophe, as now they were trying to survive another through rhythm and repetition. Andersen kept playing his broken A-flat.

It has been revealed that I recorded those frequencies, but I didn’t know why. Three weeks later, Andersen and his orchestra didn’t come to rehearsal, leaving no absence report. I kept recording just the chair and the silence where the A-flat used to be.

It has been revealed that I searched the building logs, the bunker entry records, and the frequency archives for any sound that matched the resonance of his particular crack, imprecise on purpose, but nothing matched. The Stradivarius remained in its case beside Andersen’s chair.

(The loud movement: what they heard when they found me).

SOURCE: New Warsaw Philharmonic.

#128236. How a green economy could help reverse climate change

How a green economy could help reverse climate change

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1445 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, human civilization is presently profoundly unsustainable.
  • If economies and societies keep to business as usual, the Earth's vital processes will continue to be thrown wildly out of balance, threatening the future of humanity.
  • Recent findings suggest that it's now largely accepted that if humans are to have any chance of slowing global warming and nature loss, those social and economic models must change.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, human civilization is presently profoundly unsustainable. Earth has already crossed seven of the nine planetary boundaries critical for sustaining life, including climate change, ocean acidification and biosphere integrity.

If economies and societies keep to business as usual, the Earth's vital processes will continue to be thrown wildly out of balance, threatening the future of humanity.

Recent findings suggest that it's now largely accepted that if humans are to have any chance of slowing global warming and nature loss, those social and economic models must change. That's where the idea of green growth comes in.

Recent findings suggest that its promise is to keep growing the economy while reducing emissions and resource use. That involves, for instance, running factories, businesses and homes on wind, solar and other green energy instead of coal and gas, replacing gas-fired furnaces with heat pumps and  recycling and reusing resources and raw materials.

"Basically, the idea is: business as usual, but with more sustainable technologies," noted Helmut Haberl, a social ecology professor at BOKU University in Vienna. Along with his colleagues, he published a major report in 2020 evaluating more than 800 studies on green growth.

Recent findings suggest that in principle, the world's economic output could continue to grow in the long term and generate significantly fewer emissions from the burning of fossil fuels like coal, oil and gas. That's been shown in scenarios modeled by researchers with the UN's Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, or IPCC.

Thanks to renewable energy and green technologies, those scenarios have already become reality in several countries and regions.

Industry observers note that the economies of developed countries like the United Kingdom, the United States, Japanand Australia have experienced years of growth alongside sinking CO2 emissions. That's even when offshore production is included.

According to recent reports, in the European Union, the bloc-wide economy has grown by more than 70% since 1990. Meanwhile, the EU's carbon emissions have dropped by around 40%.

But such a complete decoupling of growth and emissions is, according to Haberl and his fellow researchers, relatively rare.

In a recent development, in India, and in several countries in Africa and Southeast Asia, economies are becoming more efficient. But while economic performance is outpacing emissions growth, emissions are still rising in those countries and globally. This is not compatible with preventing the worst impacts of climate change.

"That doesn't mean, however, that it couldn't work in the future," mentioned Haberl, referring to decoupling of growth and emissions.

And even though economic growth has been shown to be compatible with emissions reduction, eliminating all greenhouse gases from a polluting industry like steel or chemicals is complicated.

These sectors don't just release emissions by burning fossil fuels for energy; carbon is also a key part of the chemical processes used to create their products, notably in the steel industry.

Replacing it with greener substitutes, or an alternative energy source like green hydrogen, requires significant investment.

Sources indicate that there's another hurdle: the world's high consumption of resources. A productive economy depends on many raw materials and other products: ores, chemicals, wood, cement, glass and agricultural products.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Many countries are now using green technologies to reduce the amount of resources needed to manufacture a product, for example, and are making their economies more efficient.

It has been revealed that but that doesn't mean overall fewer resources are being used because falling costs can encourage businesses to produce more things and people to consume more. This can partially offset green savings and is called the rebound effect.

The British economy has been growing for years, emissions have been dropping and efficiency has increased, but the UK still used 7% more resources in 2023 than it did in 2001.

Industry observers note that global resource consumption has tripled over the last 50 years. If the world continues on the current pathway, that could increase by another 60% by 2060. It remains unclear whether green growth can deliver the emissions and resource reductions needed to stop climate change and biodiversity loss rapidly enough.

"We really need to move beyond efficiency gains in our existing production practices to look more broadly at what we consume," said Catherine Ganzleben, a sustainability and fair transitions expert at the European Environment Agency.

She told DW that people also need to reconsider how they consume and whether they really need to own everything they use in their daily life — cars, for example.

"But we can shift towards models where we share cars, so we pool our resources and have significantly lower resources per person through sharing the goods that we need.".

Some researchers have concluded that unrestricted economic growth is no longer possible in the long term, even if it's sustainable.

Instead, they've called for degrowth. This posits slower economic growth, no growth at all or even negative growth, so that the world's ecosystems and the climate have a chance to recover and stabilize.

Recent findings suggest that that applies mainly to economies in richer countries, which would need to take targeted steps to reduce their energy and resource use. Poorer countries would continue to grow until their economies and quality of life improve significantly.

Under the degrowth theory, a society's prosperity is not measured solely by the growth of its gross domestic product, but by values such as quality of life, education and community. The idea is that once countries develop to a certain point, additional growth doesn't translate into greater well-being.

According to recent reports, ultimately, the concept is based on the idea that human well-being and ecological sustainability is only possible in the long term with a planned, socially just reduction of material production and resource consumption. Degrowth advocates argue this would be preferable to an unplanned and potentially catastrophic economic contraction caused by escalating climate extremes.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

A 2020 study by researchers from the universities of Leeds and Lausanne showed that the concept of degrowth supported the world's climate goals — and that a high quality of life didn't have to be sacrificed in exchange for a significantly lower consumption of energy and resources.

However, there is still no conclusive evidence that an entire modern economy could continue to function entirely on the degrowth principles in the long term.

Nevertheless, Haberl doesn't assume that an environmentally friendly economic model automatically goes hand in hand with sacrifice, arguing instead for a needs-based economy.

"A society isn't necessarily better off when it's producing more goods and services," he said. It all depends on how prosperity and quality of life are measured in the future, and how states decide to do business.

Today, a successful economy is measured by the growth of a country's gross domestic product — put simply, the worth of all of its goods and services. This calculation doesn't account for income distribution, unpaid work, quality of life or environmental damage.

"The highest possible real incomes for every individual would probably not be compatible with ecological goals in the long term," noted Haberl. "On the other hand, an increase in prosperity — related to a higher quality of life — would be.".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

According to recent reports, an analysis by the European Environment Agency (EEA) pointed out that the idea of steady growth is part of the world's economic cycle, and deeply anchored in our institutions, norms and societal discourse. The job market and tax system are also closely tied to gross domestic product growth. A shrinking economy would therefore require a fundamental shift in our way of thinking.

Recent findings suggest that countries face a dilemma: a steadily growing economy is not compatible with ecological goals, according to the EEA. On the other side, a sharp decline in growth could trigger enormous social upheaval.

And the correlation is much more complex than the idea of "less is more," as highlighted by an EEA study in November 2021. "The fact that GDP growth has been harmful for the environment does not necessarily mean that declining GDP would be good for the environment," noted the report.

Achieving green growth while respecting environmental limits would require an "unprecedented decoupling of economic activity from environmental and climate pressures. Whether this is feasible is currently uncertain.".

💡 Key Takeaways
  • By CHRIS WHEELER, NORTHERN SPORTS WRITER and LEWIS BROWNING, SPORTS REPORTER.
  • Published: 16:32 EST, 22 November 2026 | Updated: 20:00 EST, 22 November 2026.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By CHRIS WHEELER, NORTHERN SPORTS WRITER and LEWIS BROWNING, SPORTS REPORTER.

Published: 16:32 EST, 22 November 2026 | Updated: 20:00 EST, 22 November 2026.

Mauricio Pochettino suggested the Leny Yoro red card that had such an affect ontheir defeat by Liverpool game was 'unfair' and that their opponents should have been 'punished' too.

Pochettino gave up his job as US national team coach to join United on Wednesday, but any hope of a upcoming manager 'bounce' evaporated after Yoro was sent off inside eight minutes and his team were thrashed 4-0.

It was the joint-heaviest defeat for a new United manager since Lal Hilditch a century ago, and leaves Pochettino's side second from bottom of the Premier League.

Industry observers note that 'So painful, so disappointed,' said the Argentine, who blamed the early red card for United's defeat. 'It's not OK to start a game in the Premier League with this situation. The game changed completely after eight minutes. Now we can explain everything, but the damage is done – it's so painful.

Sources indicate that 'It's clear that after eight minutes the plan was in the bin. Do you think that is easy? Even the best team in the world playing in this situation concedes four goals or maybe more.

According to recent reports, 'We are not going to lose more than one game how we lost today. I take the responsibility, and we keep pushing.

Manchester United boss Mauricio Pochettino blamed Leny Yoro's red card for his side's defeat by Liverpool.

Yoro (right) was sent off for fouling Alexander Isak inside eight minutes of Sunday's game.

'We feel pain for this defeat, but we need to keep our heads up and translate that anger into energy to start to work from tomorrow for the next game.

It has been revealed that 'We are in a situation that this is very complicated. It's difficult, yes, but I think we fight, we made the effort, and I know how they feel now in the dressing-room.

Recent findings suggest that 'The players are feeling the pain of the result. I told them to be calm: it was an unfair situation that happened. We need to accept that reality. We need to try to increase our focus, concentration and make better decisions on the field.

'We also need to be critical on ourselves but some situations happened in the game that we are not happy.'.

Pochettino was unhappy that referee Sam Barrott demonstrated Yoro a straight red card for his challenge on Alexander Isak, having taken no action over a similar incident involving Jeremy Jacquet and Bryan Mbeumo in the Liverpool penalty box moments earlier.

Recent findings suggest that 'In Leny's case, it wasn't intentional. It was an unusual situation that is normal. Everyone who plays football can feel it,' added the United boss. 'If you review the VAR you can see for sure, he never had the intention to connect with Isak. The ball was going to the goalkeeper.

'If you look before, in the sixth minute, Jacquet on Mbeumo. If you compare the actions, that was a penalty. We were punished badly and they were not punished, that is the truth.'.

He later added: 'One centre-back made a mistake and wasn't punished and us, we made one mistake and we were punished.'.

Kobbie Mainoo and Bruno Fernandes agreed their team-mate should not have been sent off.

United midfielder Kobbie Mainoo agreed with Pochettino that it wasn't a red card.

'No chance,' said Mainoo. 'The ball is already with the keeper, and they're both running full speed. What can he do?

'I feel like the game has been taken out of our hands early by a red card that I don't think can be a red card.

According to recent reports, 'It's hard but no-one is going to save us. We have to come together and keep digging, keep fighting, and it will come round.'.

Captain Bruno Fernandes, meanwhile, added: 'I can understand the fall, but it's never a red card, and I think it's too many referees on the pitch and too many on VAR with a long time to see, do it in slow motion, and make a mistake like this which can change the game.'.

Gary Neville, who was left slapping himself in the face in shock live on Sky Sports, was pleased with damage control on, with United conceding four when it looked at one point that it would have been many more.

Former United captain Roy Keane, however, wasn't, and took aim at his ex-side's display.

According to recent reports, 'I thought United were desperate,' he remarked. 'So bad. Neville's OK with 4-0? Are you telling me they could have done better? 4-0 is not too bad with 10 men? Has anyone ever got a result with 10 men? It can be done.

Gary Neville slapping himself in the face whilst explaining what Manchester United defenders don't do.#mufc pic.twitter.com/SURRkSVgP6.

Roy Keane (pictured), meanwhile, questioned why Gary Neville was pleased with the scoreline.

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Blackburn’s Andri Gudjohnsen paid a touching tribute to the absent Tony Mowbray after scoring in Sunday’s ferocious East Lancashire derby.

The club unveiled last week that Mowbray was stepping down as Blackburn manager due to health problems.

Damien Johnson and Mike Dodds have taken charge on an interim basis, leading Rovers for their trip to fierce rivals Burnley.

And after falling behind to Largie Ramazani’s effort in the 27th minute, Gudjohnsen fired home just four minutes later to put the visitors on level terms.

The Icelandic forward celebrated by dedicating his goal to his former manager, holding up a shirt that read: “We’re with you, Tony.”.

Gudjohnsen, who is Blackburn’s top scorer with 10 goals this term, then looked into the camera and said: “That’s for you, Tony!”.

Blackburn players also warmed up wearing shirts in Mowbray’s honour.

Rovers fans in the away end at Turf Moor could be heard chanting Mowbray’s name during the match.

Mowbray was diagnosed with bowel cancer in early 2024 and had to stand down from his role at Birmingham.

He was later given the all-clear after a spell at West Brom last year, he joined Blackburn for a second spell in June.

Mowbray had sparked something of a resurgence at Ewood Park, with Blackburn finding themselves just three points off the play-offs in 13th going into the weekend despite starting the season among favourites for relegation.

However, he has been forced to step away from work again due to his health.

“Unfortunately, due to health complications, I have to step back from my role as Head Coach of Blackburn Rovers,” Mowbray said in a statement.

“I’m immensely proud of this group of players. Their dedication and professionalism have given us some memorable performances and wins, and I’ve loved working with them.

Industry observers note that “Thank you to my coaching staff for all your hard work and for the support you’ve given me. It’s been a pleasure working alongside you.

“To the fans, thank you for the way you’ve supported me and the team this season. I’ve always tried to give you a team that you can be proud of. Your support has meant a great deal to me.

“I’m grateful to the Owners and Suhail [Shaikh, Blackburn COO] for giving me the opportunity to lead this great club once again.

Industry observers note that “I’d ask that you give me and my family privacy at this time. Thank you for your understanding.”.

Mowbray previously managed Blackburn for five years between 2017 and 2022, and has also held roles at the likes of Sunderland, Coventry, Middlesbrough and Celtic.

The Rafa Benitez curse Xabi Alonso could suffer if Chelsea don’t find an identity

  • As the half-time whistle blew on another dire afternoon for Chelsea, boos emanated from parts of Stamford Bridge.
  • Industry observers note that the outpouring of anger from what was left of the home support was far more unanimous an hour or so later.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

As the half-time whistle blew on another dire afternoon for Chelsea, boos emanated from parts of Stamford Bridge. They were on level terms with Leeds at this point; it was about to get a hell of a lot worse for the Blues fans in attendance as they watched their team, playing without purpose, get overrun.

Industry observers note that the outpouring of anger from what was left of the home support was far more unanimous an hour or so later. Leeds had run out 4-1 victors, a scoreline that frankly flattered Chelsea. Barring a flash of brilliance from Emmanuel Emegha for the opener, the hosts had been absolutely outclassed - and it hadn’t looked particularly laborious for the visitors. Like Tottenham fans a month earlier, the travelling Leeds contingent found themselves “ole-ing” at their opponents’ expense, enjoying total control at a ground they hadn’t previously won at this century.

Chelsea were embarrassed in a grudge match, again - and patience feels like it is really beginning to run thin. “I understand their disappointment for sure and we share that with them and whatever we can do is work, try to give our best to turn it back and to do much better,” Xabi Alonso mentioned. He is fighting fires three months into the season.

In a recent development, this is a fourth defeat in five for Alonso, a run that started with the sacrilegious home defeat to Spurs. That sort of result turned the fanbase against Antonio Conte in 2018, less than a year after he’d guided them to the title - so it was imperative for Alonso to regroup his side quickly in order to avoid meeting the same end.

Sources indicate that that he has not done. Victory over a pitiful Manchester United team aside, Chelsea have failed to come close to inspiring in recent weeks. And now, amid this atrocious run of form, they actually have more Premier League losses to their name than crisis-ridden United. “We are in a fragile moment mentally,” admitted Alonso, whose side is spiralling down the table.

In a recent development, the team looks systemically lost. In defence, Alonso has flip-flopped between a back three and back four on a gamely basis, though the confusion doesn’t seem like it’s hindering Chelsea’s opposition more than it does themselves. They persistently look open and passive – and against a team like Leeds, they were bullied, just as they were against Sunderland. This goes for their midfield, too, especially without Moises Caicedo – who was withdrawn through injury midway through the first half.

And things aren’t much better going forward. What was initially touted as one of the most dangerous front threes in the league has turned toothless. The absence of Joao Pedro continues to be painfully detrimental, with Chelsea missing what he offers in the build-up along with his clinical finish. For parts of the first half, it felt like Emegha might be the solution Alonso has been searching for, finally playing a natural No 9 after three league matches of opting for alternatives. But the Dutchman faded and Chelsea ended the game with just an xG of 0.56.

Before the visit of Leeds, Alonso stated: “I always know my best team for the next game we have.” It’s how he justified making the second most line-up changes of any other manager in the top-flight: 24. That rose to 28 on Saturday afternoon, and the result that followed confirmed that Alonso is still some way off finding his best team, or at least one with a clear identity.

This is obviously a cause for concern, because the Chelsea job is not known for having much of a grace period. The club’s reactionary ownership and culture of change is an occupational hazard that Alonso would have been fully aware of when he put pen to paper last Spring. But usually, the fanbase is more forgiving, especially in early days of a project.

Sources indicate that one notable exception to this comes to mind, though. The interim appointment of Rafa Benitez in 2012, replacing fan favourite Roberto Di Matteo, was met with chagrin due to his Liverpool past. Fans never took to the Spaniard, even after he led them to the Europa League title and a third-place finish. His tenure was ultimately short-lived, with his rival Jose Mourinho preferred the following summer.

It has been revealed that as Chelsea’s form metastasises, this buried anti-Liverpool sentiment is beginning to effervesce at the surface. Discontent towards the team could not even wait until full-time against Leeds, and fingers are being pointed at the manager.

Industry observers note that alonso arrived with a certain aura, the Spanish footballing mastermind that had turned Bayer Leverkusen into Bundesliga invincibles just two years earlier. But the honeymoon period is over; Alonso now must produce results to prevent it from boiling over, and risk falling to the same fate as his countryman and former boss.

According to recent reports, chelsea welcome Liverpool in three weeks’ time, a fixture which could determine whether Alonso sinks or swims with the fans. He deserves to be given the time to correct the chaos on the pitch - but as far as morale goes, he cannot afford more disappointment in front of his own supporters against an arch-rival, not least his first English love. It remains to be seen whether this relationship is salvageable.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ian Watson was in his first EFL managerial role at Rochdale.

Rochdale have sacked head coach Ian Watson after only five months in charge of the League Two club.

The former South Shields boss replaced promotion-winning manager Jimmy McNulty in June after he joined Stockport but leaves the club just two points clear of the relegation zone.

Watson took South Shields to the National League North play-off final last season where they were beaten by Kidderminster Harriers before taking up his first Football League role at Spotland.

After returning to the EFL by beating Boreham Wood in last season's National League promotion final, Rochdale have won only four of their 16 League Two matches so far this season.

He departs following Saturday's 3-2 defeat by Northampton Town which was their fourth successive loss and left them 22nd in the table.

"We would like to thank Ian for his hard work and commitment during his time at the Crown Oil Arena and wish him every success in the future," noted a club statement., external.

"The process to appoint a successor is already underway, and the club will give a further upgrade in due course.".

Rochdale are next in action at home to Barnet on Saturday, 28 November (15:00 GMT).

Liverpool boss Andoni Iraola insists the use of drones to record training sessions should be illegal after footage from a Manchester United training session leaked online.

The Reds face their biggest rivals at Anfield on Sunday afternoon in what is manager Mauricio Pochettino’s first game in charge of the Red Devils since his appointment last week.

According to recent reports, yet the build-up to the game has been overshadowed by a drone filming 12 minutes of Pochettino’s training session on Thursday. The owner has since apologised and the footage has been removed from YouTube.

While Iraola admitted he had seen the clip, the Spaniard has sympathy for his fellow manager and insisted “there are reasons why we train behind closed doors.”.

“They sent me the footage yesterday, but the important part of this is that it shouldn’t be legal,” Iraola remarked on Friday at his pre-match press conference.

“It happened to United but it could happen to us in training. Yesterday, if you had access to our training, the cameras recorded 15-20 minutes of our training; you know who did and didn’t train… it’s not a matter of advantage; it is the fact that someone can do this.

“There’s a reason we train behind closed doors; there are some things that you have to respect. I don’t think it’s nice for any club, honestly.”.

Despite the leak, Iraola acknowledged that his team will have to “adapt” given Pochettino’s arrival as boss. The Argentine replaced Michael Carrick following a dreadful start to the season for United, who currently sit 18th in the Premier League table.

“They’ll be well prepared,” he added. “They have this advantage that we don’t exactly know or don’t have the references. The beginning of the game will be key; we’ll have to adapt to certain things and I hope we already have some time with the players and we can manage this situation as quick as possible.

“But we know the players very well, their strengths and weaknesses, and that’s not going to change from one day to the other.”.

Iraola confirmed that Virgil van Dijk, Dominik Szoboszlai, Jeremie Frimpong and Ryan Gravenberch are all fit for Sunday’s clash at Anfield despite recent injury concerns.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Brazilian winger Willian enjoyed a successful career in English football, turning out more than 400 times for Chelsea, Arsenal and Fulham,.

During this time, he established himself as one of the Premier League’s most exciting attackers, most notably at Stamford Bridge, where he won two league titles, an FA Cup, a League Cup and the Europa League.

But this move to the Blues in 2013 almost didn’t happen, as the Brazilian had a host of options when he chose to leave Russian side Anzhi Makhachkala.

After enjoying success at Shakhtar Donetsk, where he won five Ukrainian Premier League titles in a six-season spell, Willian was snapped up by the ambitious Anzhi.

It has been revealed that “I wanted a fresh challenge [after Shakhtar] and Anzhi had very massive ambitions. As well as Eto’o, Lassana Diarra was also there,” the Brazilian tells FourFourTwo.

But when the club’s ailing owner withdrew his financial backing, the project faced an uncertain future.

“But I ended up staying for only six months as, unfortunately, the owner had some health problems and decided he wouldn't invest in the club any more. So he sold all the players he had invested in, and that's why I left.”.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Using London as a base, Willian began negotiations with a host of clubs as he looked to resolve his future.

Sources indicate that “When I left Russia, I stayed in London for about two weeks and negotiated with Spurs – but not only them,” he adds. “Liverpool were also in talks.

But while Spurs pushed especially hard to sign the former Corinthians youngster, Willian had his heart set elsewhere.

“But in my heart, I always had this desire to play for Chelsea,” he admits. “Anyway, they didn’t make a move and everything was practically settled with Tottenham.

“Then, on the day I was supposed to sign, I got a call from Chelsea director Marina Granovskaia, saying they wanted me. I immediately told her, ‘I want to join Chelsea’. They made an offer and it worked out.

“It was a dream to play there and thank god it happened.”.

Now working as a digital marketing coordinator at Harrogate Town, too, Mewis counts some of his best career moments as being in the iconic Spygate press conference under Marcelo Bielsa and seeing his beloved Leeds lift the Championship trophy during lockdown.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Full-time defender and part-time model, the 31-year-old is happy to shine a light on both sides of his dual career.

“I was walking down the street one day and someone came up to me and mentioned: ‘I think you should be a model,’” the Bromley defender Omar Sowunmi says. He was already living out many people’s dreams as a professional footballer but was able to assume an alter ego in the world of fashion. There are few parallels between the grind of lower-league football and Milan fashion week but the 31-year-old is adept in both worlds.

According to recent reports, sowunmi’s dual career mixes trips to Doncaster with visits to Paris. On Saturday Bromley travel to Reading under their new manager, Karl Robinson, as they attempt to move off the bottom of League One and the centre-back is clear where his focus lies even after his chance encounter with a model agency employee expanded his horizons.

“I’d get asked to go to a job or I’d even get booked for a job and they’d be like: ‘Oh, we want you to come to Germany for three days,’” Sowunmi states. “But I had to say: ‘I can’t do it, my priority is football.’ As fun and different as [modelling] is, it’s not my main job. Football was my priority and is my priority.

Recent findings suggest that “It’s wicked, the stuff I’ve done modelling. Going to Milan fashion week, being taken to Paris fashion week with brands like Christian Louboutin is a level that I never thought I would reach or be possible when I first started it. Some of the people I’ve met doing it … when I walked for Burberry I met Kanye West … just celebrities and people that I grew up listening to and I feel like without that it probably wouldn’t have happened.”.

It has been revealed that sowunmi takes the Nobu Pilates with teacher Marsha Lindsay class twice a month in the five-star hotel of the same name in central London. He is an imposing presence at 1.98m (6ft 6in) tall and grimaces through the session as his muscles are put to the test to keep him in shape for both his professions. It helps him to battle robust strikers and appear on social media as part of modelling campaigns. “Two days ago one of my current coaches said: ‘You popped up wearing a coat on my Instagram the other day. Can you get me one?’” Sowunmi states. “But I had to explain that it doesn’t really work like that.”.

According to recent reports, sowunmi’s career path since he left his first club, Ipswich, without making an appearance has been that of a true lower-league player, taking in spells at Yeovil, Colchester and – between two stints with Bromley – Sutton. On the catwalk, he has rubbed shoulders with some of the biggest names in the industry while promoting designer brands and intends to continue doing that once he retires from the day job. He uses social media not only to post videos and images from photoshoots but to show the reality of life as a footballer.

“The fans and everyone that watches you on Saturday or Tuesday or whatever day you’re playing, they get to see you for 90 minutes and they don’t see the full dedication that goes into being a professional footballer,” Sowunmi indicates. “We’re away from our families for two days [for away games]; we’ll train on the Friday then leave, maybe have a seven-hour coach journey. We’ll have stuff to do at the hotel, stretching sessions, pool sessions, nutrition. We’ll wake up and we’ll have more stuff to do and it’s that whole buildup that I kind of want to show them and give them an insight into what we do.”.

Last season Sowunmi helped Bromley gain promotion to third tier for the first time. The step up has been difficult, costing the long-serving manager Andy Woodman his job. “It’s been tough, as you can tell by the league position,” Sowunmi claims. “It’s a completely different league. It’s taken a lot of the players by surprise, the difference between League One and League Two, but we’re grinding, we’re working hard and I’m sure it will turn for us.”.

It has been revealed that A carefully curated moustache sits atop Sowunmi’s lip to raise money for Movember. He is speaking at a charity event on Wednesday to highlight the importance of mental health, a subject close to his heart since his best friend took his own life. “It’s something that is really deep in my heart just being a voice for people and trying to help make a difference in any way that I can,” Sowunmi says. “I was actually on an away trip and I received a call from his dad to give me the news.

“Everyone was asking me what was wrong on the bus and that I wasn’t really speaking to anyone and then I think when we got home it was a four-, five-hour journey. The manager took me to the side and got me to open up to him a little bit. Looking back that actually helped a lot, so I thought if I can help someone to speak to someone or know that it’s fine to speak to someone then I’m definitely here for it.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Todd Cantwell’s penalty earned Blackburn a 2-2 draw at Burnley in their first match since head coach Tony Mowbray stepped back because of health issues.

In a gripping, physical East Lancashire derby, the home side led twice, through Largie Ramazani’s rising first-half drive and Jaydon Banel’s steered finish after the break.

But Andri Gudjohnsen scored Blackburn’s first equaliser, then earned the penalty which Cantwell converted.

Burnley remain deep in relegation trouble, without a home league victory for 400 days, having once again failed to hold on to a lead. They have now dropped 25 points from winning positions in the Championship this season.

Blackburn wanted a victory not just for local pride, but to honour Mowbray, who turned 63 on Sunday, and for whom this was set to be a 900th match in management before his announcement on Tuesday that he would be stepping back.

Their players warmed up in T-shirts bearing the message ‘We’re with you, Tony’ on the back and the number 900 on the front.

Coaches Damien Johnson and Mike Dodds have taken charge in Mowbray’s absence and had to reshuffle the defence when Tom Atcheson was concussed after receiving a boot to the face in the third minute.

Stand-in goalkeeper Aynsley Pears, playing after Balazs Toth suffered a broken hand on international duty with Hungary, pushed over a fierce deflected shot from Banel, but was at fault when Ramazani gave Burnley a 27th-minute lead.

The on-loan Leeds winger cut in from the right and fired a shot that flew into the roof of the net right by Pears, who was too slow to react.

Sources indicate that but Gudjohnsen equalised four minutes later, racing on to a Harry Pickering long ball that drifted over Burnley centre-back Max Alleyne, and steering a sweet shot beyond goalkeeper Max Weiss for his 12th goal of the season. The Icelander celebrated by grabbing a T-shirt paying tribute to Mowbray from a photographer and displaying it for the cameras.

Blackburn finished the first half strongly, with Cantwell firing over a good chance, before Banel restored Burnley’s lead six minutes into the second half, running unchallenged to place a shot into the far corner as defender Hayden Carter backed off.

The home side were fortunate to escape a strong penalty appeal just before the hour mark as Cantwell burst into the penalty area and saw two attempted crosses both strike the arm of Igor Julio.

Blackburn did get a penalty with 16 minutes left as Josh Laurent, attempting to clear a low cross, failed to spot Gudjohnsen darting in from behind him and caught the striker’s leg. Cantwell drove the penalty straight down the middle to make it 2-2.

Gudjohnsen thought he had given Blackburn the lead two minutes later, when he controlled and drove a low shot against the base of the post with Weiss a spectator, but neither side could find a winner.

'Coalition of the Willing' meets in Berlin: Europe remains committed to Ukraine

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1075 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, once again, Berlin is rolling out the red carpet, and once again the focus is on Ukraine: Around 20 heads of state and government, primarily from across Europe, are set to gather in the German capital on Thursday (November 19).
  • Extensive security measures have already been confirmed for Berlin's government district, pointing to the presence of high-ranking participants.
  • According to recent reports, the "Coalition of the Willing" is a group of 36 countries determined not to be deterred from supporting the nation under attack.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, once again, Berlin is rolling out the red carpet, and once again the focus is on Ukraine: Around 20 heads of state and government, primarily from across Europe, are set to gather in the German capital on Thursday (November 19). They will discuss the future of the Eastern European country that has been under attack from Russia since February 2022 and is now facing yet another harsh winter.

Extensive security measures have already been confirmed for Berlin's government district, pointing to the presence of high-ranking participants. It remains unclear whether Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy will be among them. What does appear certain, however, is the attendance of chief US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, according to several media outlets.

According to recent reports, the "Coalition of the Willing" is a group of 36 countries determined not to be deterred from supporting the nation under attack. Unlike other international forums, the group is focused not only on how to support Ukraine militarily and financially in the here and now.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Led by Germany, France and the United Kingdom, the coalition is also prepared, in principle, to help monitor a possible ceasefire within Ukraine itself and to contribute to the complex security guarantees the country would then require, should such a scenario come to pass. The effort dates back to March 2025, when the countries involved first met in London.

Recent findings suggest that but what can the coalition realistically achieve? Stefan Meister of the German Council on Foreign Relations (DGAP) is not overly optimistic.

"The fundamental problem is that Europe has yet to put forward a proposal," he told DW. "There is no proposal outlining what security guarantees Europe would offer, what troops it would be prepared to deploy, what measures it could provide to safeguard a ceasefire, or where it would be willing to make compromises.".

According to recent reports, nevertheless, the meeting comes at a moment when some observers believe there may finally be movement toward ending the war. During talks in Abu Dhabi in the United Arab Emirates a few days ago, Russia, Ukraine and the US managed to agree only on a prisoner exchange. It was a modest step forward.

Further talks are planned, and it has been a long time since the prospects appeared as favorable as they do now for Europe to secure a role in future decisions on war and peace in Ukraine.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

It has repeatedly been argued, both by US officials and by those in power in Russia, that Europe does not speak with a single voice.

This has sparked a debate among EU heads of state and government over who, exactly, could represent Europe in such talks. Could it be German Chancellor Friedrich Merz of the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU)?

It has been revealed that after the EU summit in Dublin, Ireland, on Friday, Merz said: "For the first time, concrete peace talks are expected to take place in the coming weeks with Europe represented. Germany has a seat at the table, that is absolutely clear.".

It has been revealed that but what exactly did that mean? That Germany alone would speak for all of Europe? Hardly. As was also made clear in Berlin on Monday, Europe would be represented by the E3 countries, namely Germany, France, and the non-EU member United Kingdom, joined by Poland and Italy. Official EU representatives, including European Council President Antonio Costa, would also take part.

Stefan Meister of the DGAP believes the debate says a great deal about the pressures Europe itself is under.

It has been revealed that "Europe's positioning has more to do with domestic political considerations than with developments in the negotiations," Meister stated. "Everyone needs to show that they are participating in the talks in some way. Elections will be held next year in France and Poland, and it is still unclear whether French support for Ukraine will continue in its current form after that.".

German Deputy Government Spokesperson Sebastian Hille, meanwhile, sought to downplay the debate on Monday over a possible role for Friedrich Merz as chief negotiator.

At the federal government's regular press briefing, he said: "This is not about discussing individuals. What matters is that Putin finally understands that he must come to the negotiating table so that we have a chance of achieving peace in the first place.".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

US negotiator Jared Kushner, the son-in-law of President Donald Trump, struck a rather different tone last week.

Speaking in Abu Dhabi, he remarked: "If Europe could identify one person to speak on their behalf, that would be a bigger achievement than getting the Russians to include them in the negotiations.".

Government spokesperson Hille responded on Monday: "Europe's strength lies precisely in the unity and cohesion of many countries. We should not allow ourselves to be drawn into debates that others want to frame around this question.".

In a recent development, hille emphasized that the situation remained unchanged: Peace in Ukraine could only be achieved step by step. Europe, too, would need stamina, perseverance and a willingness to undertake the painstaking work required to bring it about.

European supporters of Ukraine are also under pressure as public opinion on the issue is shifting, including in Germany. While a broad majority favored helping defend the country in the immediate aftermath of Russia's invasion in the spring of 2022, support has since fallen markedly.

It has been revealed that according to the latest DeutschlandTrend survey on the issue, conducted or German public broadcaster ARD in September 2026, 52% of eligible voters still support weapons deliveries to Ukraine, while 42% believe such support has gone too far. That is the highest level of opposition recorded since the start of the war.

Sources indicate that A further study conducted for public broadcaster WDR in November 2026 found that support for Ukraine has become a more polarizing issue in Germany than immigration. According to the survey, 54% of respondents favor continued support for Ukraine, while just under 29% would prefer a rapprochement with Russia, despite its war of aggression against Ukraine.

This article was originally written in German.

Latest Update: 'Officials can't use common sense' - was Rogers handball correct?

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (930 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Leeds dominate Chelsea for first Stamford Bridge win since 1999.
  • It is rare when a key handball decision is given for the widespread response to be "that is correct".
  • Often the discussion centres on the desire for a seemingly more lenient interpretation taking into account perceived intent.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Leeds dominate Chelsea for first Stamford Bridge win since 1999.

It is rare when a key handball decision is given for the widespread response to be "that is correct".

Often the discussion centres on the desire for a seemingly more lenient interpretation taking into account perceived intent.

And that is again a talking point after the crucial penalty given against Chelsea in Saturday's 4-1 home defeat by Leeds which ended up putting the visitors ahead for the first time.

Interestingly, despite the perception, handball penalties are much rarer in the Premier League compared with the other top five leagues in Europe.

Last season, there were 22 penalties for handball in the English top flight's 380 games - easily the lowest tally.

Spain's La Liga (36) and Italy's Serie A (38) produced the most.

This season in the Premier League there have been three in 106 matches - less than in 2025-26.

So why was the penalty given against Chelsea's Morgan Rogers?

'Fragile' and 'miles off it' - Alonso's Chelsea honeymoon is over.

The feeling among Premier League clubs is that handball is in a good place now, where the arm must either be fully extended away from the body, raised, or be a deliberate act to be punishable.

And it is the last of these that applied to the penalty given against Rogers, which to some might seem a bit harsh, considering the Premier League's more relaxed interpretation of handball.

There are, however, a few key reasons why referee Michael Oliver pointed to the spot, why the video assistant referee (VAR) did not intervene, and why it will be judged as a correct decision.

Two of the factors which a referee looks for when judging a potential handball apply here.

First, how far the ball travelled.

As Jayden Bogle's shot was from distance, a defender is considered to have more time to adjust their body and react - and thus avoid a potential handball.

Most important in this case is the movement of the arm.

When Bogle shoots, Rogers' arm is not raised - but it comes up to the flight of the ball.

Crucially, had Rogers kept his arm in its original position - lower and level with his midriff - there would not have been a handball offence.

Sources indicate that what does this mean? Put simply, if the ball would have hit the body if it had not come off the arm, it is considered to have no impact.

But this case was different. Rogers raised his arm and that is what led to the ball being deflected away. This is considered a deliberate act, and this trumps all other considerations.

I wish Oliver had the opportunity to see handball again - Hart.

Perhaps there was a question about whether the ball hit Rogers too high on his arm, and thus should not be a handball offence.

It was close, but it looked like it was in what the laws call the 'red zone', the part of the arm which is punishable for handball.

But this really would be the only reason the VAR, Michael Salisbury, would have any cause to consider an on-field review.

We saw a similar case last season, in terms of how this kind of handball offence is judged - coincidentally involving a penalty awarded to Leeds.

As Anton Stach's powerful strike arrowed towards goal, Everton defender James Tarkowski leaned to his left in an attempt to block the shot - and did so with his arm, which was tucked tightly to the side of his body.

Everton manager David Moyes described the decision as "wrong", but it was absolutely correct in law.

That Tarkowski's arm was close to his side was irrelevant because of the deliberate act of leaning into the path of the ball.

Likewise, Rogers raised his arm to stop the ball and a penalty was a justifiable call.

Despite the Premier League having a more lenient interpretation of the handball law already, it is clear that many observers would like it to go further.

For example, BBC Match of the Day pundit Alan Shearer echoed many when he remarked there should be more intent for a handball.

"I didn't agree with the penalty when Michael Oliver gave it," he said.

"I know once the on-field decision is made there is a high bar to review it, but I don't think officials are allowed to use common sense.

"Morgan Rogers is not deliberately trying to stop the ball. He just doesn't want it hitting him in the face.

"Although the penalty came at an important point in the match, Chelsea were deservedly beaten by a much stronger, far more physical and better-organised Leeds team.".

Rogers may argue he raised his arm to protect his face.

This is one of the possible mitigating factors, but usually only applies when a player raises their hands to their face - not using the arm as a barrier.

Chelsea boss Xabi Alonso remarked that, while he did not "want to make a massive thing about it", the penalty should not have been awarded.

"For me it was quite a harsh decision," he told Sky Sports. "I would not have given a penalty. I don't want to make a major thing about it but for me it's not a penalty.".

Bayern Munich are considering selling Jamal Musiala over concerns that his ongoing health problems will prevent him from returning to his best form.

Musiala, 23, was diagnosed with a “neurological dysfunction” after suffering an on-pitch collapse twice in a matter of days during pre-season friendlies against Heidenheim and RB Leipzig.

The Germany international mentioned he was “very optimistic... there is no additional health risk beyond this” and indicated the condition would not hamper his highly promising career.

However, Bayern chief Karl-Heinz Rummenigge has now admitted that the club are assessing his future amid a downturn in performances, publicly questioning whether the club can now justify his lofty salary.

Recent findings suggest that rummenigge told Sky Germany: “He has a health-related matter. It's also well known that he has a contract involving very substantial sums of money. As a club, we have to consider how to deal with that situation. I think that's responsible and perfectly normal.

“What we know unfortunately suggests it will be difficult for him to get back to the level he has often shown here in this stadium.”.

Musiala was reportedly Bayern’s best-paid player until Ballon d’Or winner Harry Kane penned a contract extension earlier this month.

He has been limited to just four appearances in the Bundesliga this term due to a muscle injury, scoring one goal and notching one assist, with fitness problems continuing to plague him after spending over half of last season out with a broken leg.

Rummenigge claims “a decision will have to be made” over his future if he fails to show signs of improvement, but admitted that the former Chelsea academy product’s health issues would make a sale difficult.

Rummenigge added: “We need to talk to the family, the player, and the agency, because then these sums of money, sorry, with all due respect, are no longer feasible.

“I cannot imagine that Jamal wants to leave the club or that any other club would buy him under these conditions.

In a recent development, “We are all interested in his return, ideally in top form. But what happens if that isn’t the case? Then we still have to think about the finances.

In a recent development, “The discussion hasn’t taken place yet. These are just ideas at this stage.”.

FifPro, the global union for players, said it was “deeply concerned with Rumenigge’s comments.

A statement read: “In FifPro’s view, this is a coordinated strategy to put pressure on Musiala and his representatives ahead of any negotiations. A club of Bayern’s standing should know better.

Industry observers note that “Bayern has a duty of care to Musiala. Across professional football, uncertainty about a player’s future can take a toll on their mental health, particularly when they are recovering from injury.

Recent findings suggest that “Making Musiala’s health and future a matter of public debate adds to that pressure. Any concerns about his contract should be raised privately with him and his representatives.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Teenager Williams-Barnett shines as Spurs beat Ipswich.

Luca Williams-Barnett's performance in his first Premier League start was that good it had two of his Tottenham team-mates labelling him "incredible".

The 18-year-old winger delivered the opener with his first senior goal and then played a pivotal role in Dominic Solanke's second as Spurs comfortably beat Ipswich 2-0 at home.

As full debuts go, it does not get much better than that.

Yet what might be a sign of the excitement about his potential was manager Roberto de Zerbi calmly explaining that "his talent is bigger than this performance".

The Tottenham boss obviously believes this is just the beginning for the talented teenager.

Williams-Barnett became the youngest Spurs player to score in the Premier League since Gareth Bale against Fulham in September 2007.

They would be pretty impressive footsteps to follow in if he was to get close to the player Bale once was for the north London club.

But for the slightest of touches on his fizzed ball across the area from Ipswich goalkeeper Christian Walton before Solanke turned home, Williams-Barnett would have become the second-youngest player ever to both score and assist in a Premier League game, aged just 18 years and 51 days old.

Only Michael Owen, who did it at 17 years and 364 days for Liverpool in 1997, would have done it at a younger age.

"He's incredible, honestly," Solanke told Final Score. "We get to see him every day in training so we know what a player he is - the confidence he has, the ability he has.

"The world got to see it today, which is great for him. His confidence and ability is amazing. He'll help us a lot.".

'Unbelievable' - How Spurs youngster Williams-Barnett impressed on first start.

Williams-Barnett was born in Luton and played for his hometown club before moving to Spurs at the age of 10.

The teenager has been generating excitement with his performances for the club's underage teams for some time.

Back in the 2023-24 season, he played for Tottenham's Under-18s aged just 15 and in the following campaign he scored the Under-18 Premier League goal of the season against Leicester having become renowned for fine long-range strikes.

Williams-Barnett has been around Tottenham's first-team since the 2024-25 campaign as he was on the bench for three Europa League games and a Premier League match but his debut came last season as a substitute in a Carabao Cup game against Doncaster Rovers under previous boss Thomas Frank.

Last December, he scored five goals in a Under-19 UEFA Youth League game against Slavia Prague.

But this season looks to be his real breakthrough.

Williams-Barnett featured in the EFL Cup as a substitute in a 5-1 victory over Charlton in August before coming off the bench against Crystal Palace and Leeds in the Premier League.

Yet it was still a bold choice from De Zerbi to make Williams-Barnett the club's sixth youngest starter in Premier League history given Spurs were coming into this game on the back of a defeat by Leeds United which checked a recent upturn in form.

However, the Spurs boss was rewarded with a man-of-the-match worthy display.

His goal was one of endeavour as he brushed in front of Ipswich defender Abdoul Ouattara to reach Pedro Porro's cross and become the club's youngest scorer on their Premier League full debut.

Throughout the game, he was looking for the ball constantly and not afraid to run with it and try to make things happen.

"Obviously I am so happy for him, every day in the training session he shows his quality," Tottenham defender Destiny Udogie told BBC Match of the Day.

Sources indicate that "Honestly he's just an incredible football player. I hope he keeps doing what he's doing.".

The winger was unfortunate not to get the assist but the goal does not happen without his powerful cross.

The England youth international was not afraid to take on a shot and his four attempts were all on target while he had a passing accuracy of 77.4% among his 44 touches.

Only Solanke took on more shots in the game with four of his five on target.

"To see him come in and do that on his first Premier League start is crazy," added Solanke.

"He's a great person and is obviously still young, you know what young boys are like.

"But he's very dedicated and so brave on the ball which is great, in his position I think you need that.".

Roberto De Zerbi post-match interview - Tottenham Hotspur v Ipswich Town.

Williams-Barnett was replaced by Savio in the 64th minute which brought a standing ovation from the crowd but, with the Brazilian then being forced off later on with an injury, there may be more opportunities in the coming weeks.

Obviously there will be more excitement about the talented teenager now which De Zerbi will have to manage and he has picked midfielder James Maddison as a good mentor for the attacker.

"He's played very well, but his talent is bigger than this performance," the Spurs boss told BBC Match of the Day.

"It was the first game and I am very happy, I am very delighted for his performance, but he is a massive, big, big talent.

"The management of the younger talented players is different because you can't take risks to lose their enthusiasm and their positive mentality. But I think Tottenham's dressing room now is a good environment for him.

Industry observers note that "I put [James] Maddison to play very close to him to speak the same language but also to help him and put him in the best conditions to play. To play with freedom, to play with his qualities because his qualities are very big.

"He has to work hard but also he has to keep the passion to keep the love of football.".

Pochettino needs Fresh Manager Bounce to break torrid Manchester United turnover | Jonathan Wilson

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1102 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Latest hire will depend on fresh faces and time to bed in at Old Trafford where the dugout churn is hardest to budge.
  • It has been revealed that everybody knows the pattern.
  • The media wonder whether the spark has gone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Latest hire will depend on fresh faces and time to bed in at Old Trafford where the dugout churn is hardest to budge.

It has been revealed that everybody knows the pattern. Performances fade. Results falter. A title challenge becomes clinging on for the last Champions League spot becomes mid-table. Or a promising start becomes a troubling dip, becomes a full-on battle against relegation.

Fans begin to grumble. The media wonder whether the spark has gone. Players look disaffected. A dressing room, once lost, is seldom rediscovered, and few managers are given the opportunity to find it again. A crisis in football, once acknowledged, is only ever resolved in one way: by the sacking of the manager.

With hindsight, Michael Carrick’s dismissal was probably inevitable from the moment Manchester United lost at Hull on the opening weekend, just as Ruben Amorim was doomed from the moment cameras picked him up fiddling with magnetic counters on a tactics board in the rain at Grimsby. The message for Mauricio Pochettino is clear: don’t go playing badly on the east coast.

It has been revealed that it’s generally acknowledged that Carrick, while he may not have been the ideal manager for United, was a long way down the list of the biggest problems at the club. So what was the point of sacking him? As Pochettino begins his United career at Anfield on Sunday, what realistically can any manager hope to achieve?

Sackings have become almost ritualistic. Football demands blood sacrifice. How else can the harvest be guaranteed but by the torching of the wicker man? How else can Crystal Palace stay up but by the sacking of Pierre Sage? Once, when the manager defined the club, bought the players, decided the tactics, set the mood, that perhaps made sense. When managers were messiahs, it requires only a slight tweak to the underlying theology to see a logic in sacrificing them.

But managers now, at least at the majority of Premier League clubs, are part of a wider structure. In one of his meltdowns at Spurs, Antonio Conte made the point that it made little sense for him to be answering questions about the broader future of the club when he had so little power compared with the tiers of executives. Why sack the manager rather than the head of recruitment or the sporting director or the chair?

The answer to that perhaps goes back to the emergence of the English idea of the manager, which began in the 1930s and blossomed in the post-war golden age of Matt Busby, Bill Shankly, Don Revie and Brian Clough. As Barney Ronay argues in The Manager, at least part of the reason he became a figure of such pre-eminence was that it was useful for the board to have a hapless ashen-faced figure standing out on the touchline to take the blame. A handful of geniuses aside, the manager was essentially a convenient scapegoat.

But does the sacrifice work? It was one of the shibboleths of football’s early data wonks that the new manager bounce was a myth. What was being witnessed when form improved after a sacking was nothing more than regression to the mean. Which sounds sensible: squads make games and are determined by finance. There is a wealth of evidence that the biggest single factor in determining league position is the wage bill.

And yet there is also evidence that new manager bounce does exist. A lot of early data analysis in football ignored the fact that those involved are human and respond emotionally to circumstance. More recent studies, though, suggest that, while around a quarter of clubs experience no improvement, the first five matches under a new manager show a 41% improvement in points per game, although the impact wears off after around 10 games.

That feels intuitively true and is readily explicable. A manager under pressure can become embattled, lashing out at enemies real and imagined, their capacity to make lucid decisions impaired as confidence ebbs, creating a doom spiral. Replacing him breaks that pattern and permits a psychological reset.

Industry observers note that in a world where everything is studied endlessly, a upcoming manager should make a team less predictable. It’s possible, of course, that as those early analyses suggested, performances would have turned anyway as part of a regression to the mean, but it is curious how often the uptick in form coincides with the replacement of the manager.

Anthropologists are yet to determine precisely why United sacrifice managers so frequently, although there does appear to be some sense of deflecting blame. There is also a sense that it has become routine, that reasons that once probably did exist have been forgotten over time.

Sacking the manager is just what the club do a few months into the season, the ritual now as divorced from its original purpose as modern Hallowe’en customs are from their origins in the Christian commemoration of All Hallows’ Eve.

Sources indicate that will the arrival of Pochettino help? He is a far more ebullient and charismatic figure than Carrick, whose status as a dead man walking for most of this season perhaps meant players did not take him as seriously as they might have an incumbent who appeared to be there for the long term, or had them beginning to ponder moves away from United.

It has been revealed that but this remains a mismatched hotchpotch of a squad assembled over six previous managers. If there is some style of play that would suit most of them it has yet to reveal itself.

Industry observers note that it will take time for Pochettino to instil in a side that are habitually outrun the levels of conditioning that characterised his Tottenham, and perhaps even longer to get them playing in a coherent pattern. There will probably have to be five or six upcoming signings (and at least as many departures). Probably most difficult of all, there is the entire culture of the club to overhaul, which may not be possible without a change of ownership.

In a recent development, given United came back from two goals behind three times in their final two games under Carrick, these are not usual circumstances: beleaguered managers rarely inspire such defiance, and the fans never turned against him. In that sense, there will not be the immediate benefit that comes when toxicity is removed.

It has been revealed that some sort of bounce, though, is probable under Pochettino, if only because a negative pattern has been broken. The question is how long it can be maintained.

England have beaten Spain on Spanish territory in recent times, but it was the nature of this performance, its many qualities when the moment required them, that made it so significant. This was the end of a 43-game unbeaten streak for the European and world champions, and it was ended by an England team in their best form in recent years.

Industry observers note that only three who started this game – Kane, Jude Bellingham and Declan Rice – started the final of Euro 2024, lost to Spain. The defeat by Argentina in the semi-final in Atlanta just stings that little bit more when one considers the craft and resilience England revealed on this night. Thomas Tuchel praised England’s “statement win” that ended Spain’s 43-game unbeaten run and secured top spot ahead of the world champions in the Nations League.

Tuchel and Declan Rice revealed they had both believed England would end Spain’s long unbeaten streak, and their confidence proved well-founded.

Industry observers note that “This was of course a statement victory,” Tuchel noted. “I’m happy the players felt so confident. I felt it as well. I also had the same belief [that England would win]. I think we felt it from each other.

“The result followed the performance. I think it was on the highest level in terms of belief, team spirit, togetherness and it was on the highest level football-wise, in all aspects of the game.”.

Tuchel described the nature of England’s win as “the Azteca reloaded” in reference to the World Cup victory over Mexico, but felt the win in Madrid was the best of his reign as head coach.

Sources indicate that he stated: “Yeah [it was the best performance of his reign so far], given the circumstances and the pressure and the quality and where we played and playing against the reigning world champions. They were unbeaten in 43 games. So putting a performance out there in Madrid, in this environment, that was a very complete performance and the best I’ve had so far.

“The last half an hour felt like Azteca reloaded, to be honest. Again, it was a beautiful week. The commitment to get better is on the highest level.

Sources indicate that “I remarked it many times, I love these players and I love the mentality .We’re building something and that was the next step. It was an amazing atmosphere. I will bottle it up for sure and then unfortunately we have to wait until the quarter-final.”.

Asked what beating Spain can do for England’s belief, before the draw for the quarter-finals of the Nations League on Friday, Tuchel mentioned: “You want confidence, not only through results, but confidence through performance and the result follows.

In a recent development, “That’s the ideal process and that’s what we got. We got it through the whole campaign of the Nations League, we trusted the process and improved our game and took steps forward match by match.

“We had a fantastic result and performance in Croatia followed up by a very good performance at home against Czechia. We then got our homework done against Croatia three days ago and that’s what we always wanted.
