A simple supplement could help your immune system fight cancer and viral infections

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1843 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A common amino acid found in everyday foods could play a surprisingly notable role in helping the immune system recognize cancer and fight viral infections.
  • Arginine is an amino acid that the body produces naturally and also obtains from protein-rich foods.
  • According to recent reports, now, latest research suggests that restoring arginine levels could help the immune system respond more effectively to serious threats.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A common amino acid found in everyday foods could play a surprisingly notable role in helping the immune system recognize cancer and fight viral infections. Scientists at Rockefeller University have discovered that when the body runs low on arginine, a key part of its immune defense system can stop working properly, potentially allowing dangerous cells and viruses to escape detection.

Arginine is an amino acid that the body produces naturally and also obtains from protein-rich foods. It is essential for making proteins that perform countless functions throughout the body. Researchers have long known that unusually low arginine levels are associated with several diseases, including colon cancer, but exactly how this shortage affects the body's defenses has remained unclear.

According to recent reports, now, latest research suggests that restoring arginine levels could help the immune system respond more effectively to serious threats. In experiments involving mice, increasing dietary arginine reduced the formation of colon cancer tumors and lessened the severity of influenza and SARS-CoV-2 infections. Remarkably, providing arginine after mice had already contracted influenza also improved their outcomes.

According to recent reports, the findings, published in the journal Cell, raise the possibility that an inexpensive, readily available supplement could eventually become a useful addition to cancer treatments and strategies for combating viral infections. However, further research in humans is needed to determine whether the benefits observed in mice translate into effective treatments for people.

How a Missing Nutrient Could Help Cancer Escape the Immune System.

Industry observers note that the research was led by Sohail Tavazoie, who directs the Elizabeth and Vincent Meyer Laboratory of Systems Cancer Biology at Rockefeller University. His team has spent years investigating how arginine influences cancer development and progression.

Industry observers note that in 2023, the researchers discovered that depriving colon cancer cells of arginine caused them to accumulate more genetic mutations. These changes can contribute to the unpredictable behavior of cancer cells, raising important questions about how arginine shortages might influence the disease.

It has been revealed that the latest study reveals another potentially significant consequence. When arginine becomes scarce, cells struggle to produce enough of a crucial immune system protein known as MHC-1. This protein acts as a warning system, helping immune cells identify potential dangers such as cancerous changes or viral infections.

Without enough MHC-1, abnormal or infected cells may become harder for the immune system to recognize.

Encouragingly, the researchers also found that supplying a moderate amount of arginine, comparable to the quantity available in a couple of over-the-counter supplement tablets, could help restore production of this important protein.

In a recent development, "Our work reveals how a lack of arginine interferes with the immune system, and suggests that upping arginine intake could prove beneficial," says first author Qiushuang Wu, a postdoc in the lab. "Perhaps that means it could be used in combination with other therapies to treat both cancer and viral infections.".

"Arginine supplementation could be readily tested in patients receiving immunotherapies or given to high-risk populations exposed to viral pathogens," Tavazoie suggests. "Considering that arginine is inexpensive and readily available, we hope that therapeutic and preventative studies could be undertaken soon.".

The Surprising Connection Between Arginine and Immune Defenses.

To understand why arginine has such an vital effect, the researchers investigated how cells use amino acids to manufacture proteins.

In a recent development, proteins are built from amino acids according to genetic instructions encoded in DNA. These instructions are copied into messenger RNA, which carries the information to the cellular machinery responsible for protein production.

Recent findings suggest that the instructions are read in groups of three genetic letters called codons. Each codon specifies an amino acid or provides another signal needed during protein production. Arginine is unusual in that six different codons can specify it, reflecting the multiple ways its incorporation into proteins can be encoded.

Sources indicate that scientists already knew that changes in amino acid availability could affect cellular metabolism and signaling, two processes that help regulate how cells obtain energy and respond to their surroundings. What remained less clear was whether shortages of particular amino acids could directly influence which proteins cells produce.

To investigate, Wu examined the effects of arginine availability across several disease models, including colon cancer, influenza, and SARS-CoV-2. Each of these diseases has previously been associated with abnormal levels of various amino acids.

The research was supported in part by the Stavros Niarchos Foundation (SNF) Institute for Global Infectious Disease Research at The Rockefeller University and the Weill Cancer East Hub.

"One of the most dramatic patterns to emerge was that arginine was the most depleted amino acid in all of these diseases," she says.

Why Low Arginine Levels Can Disrupt the Immune System.

Recent findings suggest that in laboratory experiments using cultured cells, Wu examined how arginine shortages affected protein production. She identified 414 proteins whose levels dropped abnormally when arginine was scarce.

According to recent reports, many of these proteins were associated with biological functions already known to depend on arginine. However, the researchers uncovered a more unexpected effect involving three genes from the HLA family.

These genes provide instructions for producing proteins associated with MHC-I (major histocompatibility complex class I), an essential component of the immune system's ability to recognize threats.

Industry observers note that MHC-I proteins are displayed on the surfaces of cells throughout the body. They act somewhat like identification displays, presenting small fragments of proteins from inside the cell to immune cells known as T cells.

When these displays reveal suspicious material, such as proteins produced by a virus or abnormal proteins associated with cancer, T cells can recognize the danger and help coordinate an immune response.

But the researchers found that arginine deficiency interfered with the production of these molecular warning signals.

Sources indicate that the reason involved ribosomes, the tiny cellular machines that assemble proteins by following genetic instructions. Because the proteins involved in MHC-I production require arginine at numerous points, the researchers suspected that an insufficient supply could interfere with their assembly.

According to recent reports, further experiments confirmed that suspicion. When arginine was unavailable, ribosomes stalled while trying to manufacture MHC-I proteins. Without enough of the required amino acid, the cells could not efficiently complete the process.

Recent findings suggest that as a result, fewer MHC-I proteins reached the cell surface, reducing the signals that would normally alert T cells to cancer-associated or viral proteins. This created an opportunity for dangerous cells to avoid immune detection.

"These findings are exciting because they reveal that consumption of a specific amino acid can directly regulate gene expression in an organism by increasing production of a protein enriched in that amino acid," Tavazoie claims. "We believe that such selective translational tuning of gene expression through dietary manipulation likely extends to many other proteins and amino acids.".

More Arginine Meant Fewer Colon Cancer Tumors in Mice.

After identifying the molecular mechanism, Wu investigated whether changing the amount of arginine in an animal's diet could influence disease outcomes.

Mice receiving diets low in arginine developed more colon cancer tumors. In contrast, mice consuming higher amounts of the amino acid developed fewer tumors.

These findings provided evidence that arginine availability can influence cancer development through its effects on the immune system, rather than simply changing how individual cancer cells behave.

The results also raised a broader question: If arginine helps immune cells recognize cancer, could it provide similar benefits when the body encounters dangerous viruses?

Arginine Also Improved Outcomes From Influenza and COVID-19 Viruses.

To explore that possibility, Wu collaborated with Heinz-Heinrich Hoffman, a research assistant professor in Charles Rice's Laboratory of Virology and Infectious Disease.

Together, they examined the effects of dietary arginine in mouse models of influenza and SARS-CoV-2, the virus responsible for COVID-19.

It has been revealed that the findings followed the same general pattern seen in the colon cancer experiments. Mice consuming more arginine experienced less severe symptoms from viral infections, suggesting that adequate levels of the amino acid helped support the body's immune defenses.

The researchers then made an even more surprising discovery.

Recent findings suggest that arginine did not appear to be beneficial only when consumed before an infection. Giving mice additional arginine after they had already been infected with influenza also improved their outcomes.

In a recent development, "Not only did mice with an arginine-rich diet have milder symptoms from viral infections, giving the mice arginine after influenza infection improved their outcomes too," Wu notes. "That was very surprising. From our genetic models, we knew manipulating arginine levels had a strong effect on gene expression, but we didn't expect the dietary manipulation to be equally impactful.".

The observation suggests that changing nutrient availability might influence how the immune system responds even after a viral infection has taken hold.

Could a Simple Supplement Improve Cancer and Virus Treatments?

The discovery has potentially key implications for understanding why some people become more vulnerable to cancer and severe viral infections.

Arginine levels naturally decline with age, and inadequate nutrition can further reduce the amount available to cells. The researchers suspect that these changes may contribute to the weakening of immune defenses seen in certain diseases and in older adults.

In a recent development, "Qiushuang's findings illuminate how poor diet and aging -- during which arginine levels naturally decline -- could create the perfect storm for the initiation of colon cancer. Similarly, age-related arginine loss could partially contribute to the greater mortality caused by respiratory viruses," Tavazoie states. "We're also investigating whether making dietary changes in other amino acids has beneficial effects in a variety of disease contexts. There are no doubt more discoveries to come.".

The possibility of using arginine alongside existing cancer immunotherapies is particularly intriguing. These treatments work by helping the immune system recognize and attack cancer cells. If low arginine levels interfere with the molecular signals required for that recognition, restoring the nutrient might help some treatments work more effectively.

The researchers also see potential for investigating arginine supplementation in people at elevated risk of respiratory viral infections.

For now, these possibilities remain experimental. The findings do not establish that taking arginine supplements prevents or treats cancer, influenza, or COVID-19 in humans.

Industry observers note that nevertheless, the research reveals an key connection between nutrition and immunity. Rather than simply providing the raw materials needed to build proteins, specific amino acids may help determine how effectively the body's immune defenses identify and respond to dangerous threats.

And because arginine is inexpensive and widely available, the discovery could provide a practical starting point for future studies aimed at strengthening the immune system against cancer and infectious diseases.

Paris St-Germain forward Desire Doue will have surgery later this month after rupturing the anterior cruciate ligament in his right knee.

The 21-year-old was in tears as he was taken off on a stretcher towards the end of the first half in the Ligue 1 champions' 3-2 victory over Nice on Saturday night.

Doue, who has arguably been PSG's best player this season, twisted awkwardly and went down under no contact.

The match was stopped for five minutes as Doue - who was visibly in pain - received treatment before he was applauded off by the crowd at the Allianz Riviera Stadium.

The European champions have been plagued with injury complications so far this season and are already without Khvicha Kvaratskhelia, who sustained an ACL injury of his own against Barcelona in October.

PSG return to action on Wednesday, when they host Roma in the Champions League.

Industry News: What's next for NASA interstellar Voyager 1 probe after passing 1 light-day from Earth?

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Voyager 1 has reached a historic milestone in space — it now takes a light-day to send a command to the spacecraft, meaning a full 24 hours for Earth to hail the distant spacecraft.
  • It has been revealed that since Voyager 1 and its twin, Voyager 2, debuted on an initial tour through the outer solar system in 1977, their missions have been packed with science.
  • According to recent reports, voyager 1's faster path out of the solar system brought it to one light-day in distance on Wednesday (Nov.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Voyager 1 has reached a historic milestone in space — it now takes a light-day to send a command to the spacecraft, meaning a full 24 hours for Earth to hail the distant spacecraft.

It has been revealed that since Voyager 1 and its twin, Voyager 2, debuted on an initial tour through the outer solar system in 1977, their missions have been packed with science. Voyager 1 looked at Jupiter and Saturn from up close before veering for a flyby of Saturn's moon Titan and Saturn's rings, a pathway that brought it above the plane of the solar system in the early 1980s.

According to recent reports, voyager 1's faster path out of the solar system brought it to one light-day in distance on Wednesday (Nov. 18), while Voyager 2 — which took a slightly slower track to see Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune — will reach a light-day of distance in 2035. So what's next for the two Voyager spacecraft as they reach further into interstellar space?

Interstellar space, which is the area where the sun's constant stream of solar particles within the heliopause gives way to the physics of interstellar space, has been a valuable harvest for both Voyagers. Voyager 1 crossed interstellar space in August 2012 and continues to get data, while Voyager 2 has done the same since November 2018.

"Current science is continuing our investigation on magnetic field strength and direction, plasma density, and energetic particle detection. What is notable is to measure how these phenomena change as the spacecraft travels further away from the sun," Suzanne Dodd, project manager for the Voyager missions at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), told Space.com in an email.

Added to that will be the Voyagers' examinations of plasma and magnetic fields nearby the spacecraft, and a focus on any "solar effects" such as shocks or pressure fronts, added JPL project scientist Linda Spilker in an email.

Industry observers note that "Key Voyager science going forward includes observing the extent to which our sun continues to affect interstellar space, all the way out to Voyager 1," Spilker continued. "Where does the sun's influence end and pristine interstellar space begin? Perhaps Voyager may last long enough to answer that question.".

According to recent reports, the team also wants to watch the magnetic field around the spacecraft continue to change direction from the sun, to interstellar space, Spilker noted. That finding was not expected when the Voyagers introduced, so scientists are curious to know more — as long as the spacecraft can last, that is.

Each Voyager continues to lose 4 watts of power a year; their launch power was 470 watts in 1977, and the nuclear power source continues to dwindle, requiring harder choices as the missions approach their 50th years of operations. Instruments have had to be shut off, and both the spacecraft were directed to perform a "Substantial Bang" of power redistribution earlier this year to preserve as much power as possible without sacrificing science.

Looking forward, Dodd states the team does not anticipate having to make any major changes to spacecraft operations until after the 50th anniversary passes for each spacecraft next August and September (as Voyager 2 launched a few weeks before Voyager 1).

A JPL representative added that the "Big Bang" should keep the remaining science instruments going until that point, although "there is also the thermal state of the spacecraft to balance." The representative added that the margins for power remain "very thin," especially as the spacecraft are quite cold in interstellar space.

"Then there are the things the team can't predict, such as the unexpected loss of contact that happened recently," the spokesperson added, referring to an approximately 48-hour glitch in which Voyager 1 suddenly stopped responding to commands last month — although the spacecraft did promptly recover.

"The goal of the mission is science, so the team is not just concerned with keeping in contact with the Voyagers, but keeping the science instruments going as long as possible," the representative added. "The further away the spacecraft get from Earth, the more they learn about how interstellar space changes further away from the heliopause.".

It has been revealed that voyager 1 team members now represent multiple generations of engineers, each one of them with distinct but essential roles. Even the most junior members of the team—Nshan Kazaryan and Bhavana Gupta—are taking on key roles in anticipation of more responsibility in the future, according to JPL mission manager Kareem Badaruddin.

Industry observers note that "They have demonstrated their value to the team consistently," Badaruddin stated in an email. Kazaryan's responsibilities include negotiating tracking schedules with the Deep Space Network (DSN), a set of three antennas for following distant missions, to keep tabs on the Voyagers. Gupta, meanwhile, has provided documentation to gather notable details from the Voyagers' command and control systems to "give detailed instructions" in case of concerns.

Industry observers note that "One of our most senior team members, Jack Lippincott, has provided critical knowledge and understanding of DSN operations and data interpretation," Badaruddin added. Pointing to one of the DSN antennas in Goldstone, California, he said the weather in that region "has been violent the last few weeks, and he has helped us to understand how to deal with unique problems that arose because of it.".

It has been revealed that while there's no real sense of how much further the spacecraft could keep going, the team indicates it's committed to be there as long as possible. "It has taken decades of exceptional engineering to get Voyager 1 to the one light-day milestone, and hopefully much further before the mission ends," Dodd said.

Badaruddin added: "One of the reasons that one light-day is so special is that it has never happened before that we were in contact with a spacecraft at this distance, and it may never happen again.".

Industry observers note that editor's note: This article was updated at 9 a.m. EST, Nov. 20, to correct the location of one of the DSN facilities to Goldstone, California (not Australia).

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Leaders of several U.S. electric vehicle manufacturers said they're not counting on increased federal support for their businesses once Democrats gain control of Congress in January, but they said they'll gladly take it if it does happen.

That was the overall sentiment from CEOs of Rivian Automotive, Lucid Group and EV startup Scout Motors during interviews with CNBC after Democrats' historic midterm election wins.

"We've honestly constructed Scout from day one to be in an environment where we're not going to count on, let's say, legislation or count on things that may or may not be there," Scout CEO Scott Keogh, an automotive veteran, told CNBC on Wednesday.

EV makers have had to contend with flip-flopping support from Washington over the years. The Trump administration has ended or rolled back support for climate change initiatives and EVs that were supported by the Biden administration, including an up to $7,500 customer incentive for purchasing an EV.

Legacy automakers such as General Motors and EV startups alike had counted on such credits to help them boost their sales and assist in electric vehicle profitability. But now they don't have that same level of federal assistance.

Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe said it's his hope that the Democratic-controlled Congress and Republican President Donald Trump can find middle ground to make progress for the EV industry, but Rivian's not counting on that.

In a recent development, "We try not to plan for those sort of things. The reality is it's probably going to have less of an impact than we think," Scaringe stated Nov. 6 following the election results. "I think we're going to actually have a lot of challenges getting things done.".

Fellow EV manufacturer Lucid, which is backed by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, is taking a similar approach.

Sources indicate that "You know, they say, 'Strategy for the worst and … hope for the best.' That's all we can say," Lucid CEO Silvio Napoli told CNBC on Monday. "Anything positive, we'll take it.".

The lack of expected support comes as Democrats seem to be more focused on hot topics such as healthcare and data centers rather than climate change and support for alternative energy technologies such as EVs.

Recent findings suggest that CNBC previously reported that House Democrats plan to bring to the floor bills reinstating the enhanced health insurance subsidies that expired under the GOP-held Congress and reversing the Medicaid cuts Trump signed into law last year. They also plan to focus on oversight of the Trump administration and affordability.

Rachel McCleery, executive director of the nonprofit policy advisory Coalition for Reimagined Mobility at SAFE, noted she believes affordability concerns also could include the cost of vehicles, including EVs.

It has been revealed that "I fully expect there will be legislative debates over what to do moving forward, including on EV and EV supply chain incentives," McCleery, a former U.S. Department of Treasury senior advisor and Ford Motor policy director, remarked. "Bringing down the cost of vehicles for U.S. consumers is top of mind for Democratic policymakers, and electric vehicles are a critical aspect of this agenda because of the multiple challenges greater EV adoption solves for.".

Scout's Keogh said if legislators decide to offer any type of support, he would prefer it to be for EV production, which could then have a trickle-down effect on vehicle pricing and help companies amid inflated costs.

Industry observers note that "I always prefer it on the production side," Keogh remarked. "Anything that can drive down production cost is going to, of course, get passed along to the customer.".

Affordability has been a concern for EV adoption as the vehicles typically cost more than traditional models with internal combustion engines.

Sales of EVs spiked last year ahead of the Trump administration ending the up to $7,500 incentive after September 2025, but have since come down from that high.

Sources indicate that cox Automotive reports the average price for a new electric vehicle as of September was more than $54,800, according to the most recent available data. That compared to the average overall industry at just over $51,100 last month.

It has been revealed that "Ultimately, incentives can help accelerate adoption, but the industry can't build its long-term strategy around them," Stephanie Valdez Streaty, Cox director of industry insight, mentioned Friday. "The goal has to be making EVs affordable and compelling enough that they make sense for more consumers with or without an incentive.".

No mention of fossil fuels in latest COP31 draft deal

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1090 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Climate negotiators have removed any mention of fossil fuels — the main source of greenhouse gas emissions heating the planet — in a new draft deal published by COP31 summit co-host Australia.
  • The latest text released Thursday at the UN climate conference in Turkey stripped out two references to a transition away from coal, oil and gas and a call for an accelerated phaseout that had been in an earlier draft.
  • This slimmed down version follows days of tough negotiations, with representatives from nearly 200 nations debating problems such as the future of fossil fuels and climate funding for developing countries.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Climate negotiators have removed any mention of fossil fuels — the main source of greenhouse gas emissions heating the planet — in a new draft deal published by COP31 summit co-host Australia.

The latest text released Thursday at the UN climate conference in Turkey stripped out two references to a transition away from coal, oil and gas and a call for an accelerated phaseout that had been in an earlier draft.

This slimmed down version follows days of tough negotiations, with representatives from nearly 200 nations debating problems such as the future of fossil fuels and climate funding for developing countries.

The text still includes a call to increase the global share of final energy demand met by electricity to 35% by 2035 — up from around 20% today — a proposal that was pushed by host Turkey.

It did not specify whether that additional electricity needs to come from clean sources rather than fossil fuels, a point that has drawn criticism from some countries.

The draft did mention the electrification target alongside efforts to triple renewable energy capacity globally as well as other energy efficiency measures. But Jan Kowalzig, a climate finance expert with Oxfam Germany, mentioned negotiators had failed to "meaningfully" link them.

Kowalzig also criticized the text for not referencing a transition away from fossil fuels in a gradual manner — something that had been mentioned in the final decision out of the COP28 in Dubai several years ago.

"This is insufficient for a climate conference that already decided several years ago to phase out fossil fuels and that presents itself as a conference focused on implementation," he said in a statement.

Another hotly contested issue at the talks has been financial support to help developing countries deal with climate change. Divisions largely revolve around who should bear the costs and whether funding should come in the form of grants or loans.

The second draft called for further discussions on a tripling of funding for climate adaptation measures in developing countries. It also noted "with concern the gap between climate finance flows and needs," with the adaptation costs in developing countries estimated at $305 billion annually up to 2035.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

The wording on finance prompted criticism from Meenakshi Raman, the coordinator of the climate change program at the Third World Network, who had been "hoping to see much more ambition on the side of finance from the developed world.".

"Coming here really confirmed the worst fears that developed countries are not only backsliding but putting nothing in terms of real meaning on the table," said Raman.

The European Union has noted it won't agree to higher climate financing pledges because it pays its "fair share" while others don't.

The draft text also expressed "deep concern" that global warming is projected to exceed 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial levels — the threshold outlined in the 2015 Paris Agreement to avoid runaway climate change.

It acknowledged that every increment of warming above current levels would "result in increasingly adverse, and in some cases irreversible, impacts and risks to human and natural systems.".

Australian Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen mentioned the text aimed to communicate that "1.5 degrees of warming is not acceptable and will not be allowed to stand.".

The draft also recognized the need for "deep, rapid ​and ‌sustained" cuts to greenhouse gas emissions and called for efforts to ramp up action targeting the potent greenhouse gas methane.

The greenhouse gas emissions heating the planet are largely caused by burning fossil fuels.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

The text additionally calls for the deployment of technologies that can remove carbon from the atmosphere to be sped up, many of which have yet to be tested and proven on a large scale.

Harjeet Singh of the Fill the Fund campaign to boost climate finance for developing countries said the second draft "trims away inconvenient mandates and accountability while leaving behind lofty rhetoric that won't protect a single vulnerable community.".

The climate conference officially ends on Friday, but it's not uncommon for the annual talks to run on for longer than expected. The latest text is expected to face further revisions before it can be adopted.

Decisions on the language need approval from all countries, meaning an objection from one party is enough to scupper a deal.

On Thursday, Panama noted it would block any agreement that does not meet its demands for a cap on oil production and steps to eliminate methane.

The country's environment minister, Juan Carlos Navarro, noted Panama would "not lend its name" to "complacent or ineffective language" in the final pact.

Australian Energy Minister Bowen stated he expected countries to bring forward their concerns, feedback and questions in the coming hours and overnight.

"We won't be leaving the rooms of Antalya until we have that consensus, until we have a plan we can put to the parties on behalf of the countries and governments they represent, and they can say, yes, we can do this: we can keep the world to 1.5 degrees of warming.".

The stakes are high for this edition of the COP summit, which comes in a year of major climate-related disasters, from wildfires and deadly heat waves in Europe to a glacier collapse in Nepal that killed more than 1,400 people.

It's also taking place against the backdrop of an intensifying "super" El Nino weather pattern, and geopolitical shocks that have sent energy prices rising globally.

It has been revealed that the conference is the first to be held under the acknowledgement by the UN that keeping the average global temperature under 1.5C is no longer realistic. Instead, scientists are talking about limiting the time spent above this threshold and bringing temperatures back down rapidly by the end of the century.

Countries are at odds about how to acknowledge overshoot of the temperature threshold in the final agreement, with some worrying that fossil fuel producing countries such as Saudi Arabia and Iran are seeking to jettison 1.5C entirely, which could lead to "backsliding" on climate action, according to AFP.

"It's critically notable for this COP to recognize, and this is really the first COP that will likely do so, that we are on the way to overshooting 1.5 degrees," remarked David Waskow, the director of the World Resources Institute's International Climate Initiative.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Not since the emergence of a certain Harry Kane has there been this much excitement about a player from Tottenham’s academy.
  • That made it four league victories from their last five matches for Roberto De Zerbi’s side and the Italian could only have enjoyed the view from the stands as he served his one-match touchline ban.
  • According to recent reports, harry Winks was the last academy graduate to score on his debut more than a decade ago – a feat that Kane also achieved two years earlier against Sunderland.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Not since the emergence of a certain Harry Kane has there been this much excitement about a player from Tottenham’s academy. On his first senior start, Luca Williams-Barnett showed just why as the 18-year-old became their youngest Premier League goalscorer since Gareth Bale in 2007 before teeing up Dominic Solanke with a mesmerising and match-winning assist against Ipswich.

That made it four league victories from their last five matches for Roberto De Zerbi’s side and the Italian could only have enjoyed the view from the stands as he served his one-match touchline ban. Tottenham have struggled to match their London rivals Arsenal and Chelsea’s record of producing homegrown players in recent years but they appear to have struck gold with Williams-Barnett.

According to recent reports, harry Winks was the last academy graduate to score on his debut more than a decade ago – a feat that Kane also achieved two years earlier against Sunderland. Yet after Spurs decided to allow the England Under-21s striker Will Lankshear to join Middlesbrough in the summer, there was no chance that Williams-Barnett would be allowed to follow him out of the door. He became the 900th player ever to represent Spurs when he made his debut last year and the teenager left the field here to a standing ovation that he will never forget.

Sources indicate that “I told him to play like he plays in the park with his friends, with the same freedom,” said De Zerbi. “And to play and to work hard without the ball, like [Ousmane] Dembélé, like Raphinha, like [Lamine] Yamal. Luca is a special player. I’m not surprised because his talent is bigger than you think. He’s very young but at same time he’s very mature. He is older than his age.”.

According to recent reports, asked whether his protege has the potential to be compared to the Barcelona sensation Lamine Yamal, De Zerbi added: “Yes, I think so. One of the best things in my career I’ve seen today on the bus to the stadium. He was watching [clips] on YouTube of Ronaldinho, Hazard. I think he’s a special guy, because if one hour before you are debuting in the Premier League, you are watching Ronaldinho, Hazard, Neymar, all these types of talent. Having the qualities is one thing but he has the passion for football, too.”.

After a promising start to the campaign, Ipswich’s momentum has stalled – they have now gone five games without a victory. But Gary O’Neil, who has already seen 16-year-old Max Dowman score twice for Arsenal against his side in the Carabao Cup, acknowledged that they had been second best throughout. “You need things to be perfect when we come to a place like this and we didn’t make things easy for ourselves,” he said.

In a recent development, de Zerbi dropped a huge hint that Williams-Barnett could be handed his opportunity to start after two impressive cameos against Crystal Palace and Leeds. “Maybe, maybe,” he stated on Friday. It turned out that the decision was actually taken last week, although the absence of Sandro Tonali due to illness forced Spurs into a reshuffle in midfield as Mateus Fernandes was handed the holding role.

Solanke has struggled to fill the void left by Kane since joining from Bournemouth in 2024 but looked in determined mood and he was inches wide with a swivel and shot from inside the area. A driving run from Williams-Barnett had the home supporters off their feet, with Solanke again going close from the resulting corner. It then needed a timely block from the teenager to stop Ipswich breaking downfield.

According to recent reports, his major moment arrived less than 60 seconds later. Porro’s ball to the back post should have been dealt with by Abdoul Ouattara, only for a moment’s hesitation to allow Williams-Barnett to muscle in front of him and apply the finish with his knee. “He’s one of our own,” sang the Tottenham fans in delight.

Sources indicate that mohammed Kudus was unfortunate to see his superb effort from a free-kick cannon off the inside of the post and away to safety. Williams-Barnett will be disappointed not to have scored his second when he miskicked inside the six-yard box with the goal gaping. James Maddison was then denied by a brilliant save from Christian Walton and Williams-Barnett left the field at half-time looking very pleased with himself as he waved to his family in the crowd.

His smile grew even broader after Darnell Furlong was left bamboozled by a direct run down the left flank before the youngster delivered the ball on a plate for Solanke to score his first goal here since March. The defeat could have been worse for Ipswich had it not been for Walton, and O’Neil will know they are in danger of being sucked into trouble if this winless run continues. There are no such concerns for Tottenham these days. Thanks to Williams-Barnett, their future looks much brighter than a few weeks ago.

Hailey Bieber knows what she’s talking about.

After the Rhode founder received criticism for saying during a recent sit-down interview that it was “optimistical delusion” that allowed her to sell her business to e.l.f. Beauty for $1 billion, she had the perfect response for internet trolls claiming she used a word that doesn’t exist.

Recent findings suggest that in a screenshot shared to her Instagram Stories Nov. 20, Bieber shared the dictionary definition of “optimistical,” which is described as “a version of optimistic.”.

Clapping back at those who gave her some flak for using the word, the 29-year-old wrote over the image, “anyways….”.

Sources indicate that bieber made the remark during her appearance at the Fresh York Times’ DealBook Summit in New York City Nov. 18, where she shared further insight into the May 2025 sale of her beauty organization.

“A billion dollars was the number that I said I would not sell it for less than that,” she said. “That felt crazy, that’s like shooting for the stars, stars, stars, stars, stars.”.

As for what made the goal possible, the beauty mogul credited “delusion.”.

She added, “You have to have a certain sense of optimistical delusion I think.”.

Soon after her remarks, internet owners took to social media to criticize Bieber over her word choice.

"'Optimistical' my eye is twitching," one user wrote on X, while another added, "Why does she think 'optimistical' is a word.".

But the beauty mogul—who shares 2-year-old son Jack with husband Justin Bieber—is no stranger to facing the haters. After all, she also spoke about building thick skin during her time in the public eye.

“I think there’s a resilience that you build,” she explained at the summit, “with so much time of enduring and going through such intense scrutiny and being so perceived all the time.”.

And although she does her best to do “internal regulation” when it comes to social media, she stressed that blocking out noise is still a work in progress for her.

According to recent reports, “I’m just someone who pays attention,” she continued. “I’m not that girl that can be like, ‘Yeah, I’m just gonna ignore it.’ I don’t work that way. I’m too sensitive and I care too much to try to be that person that it doesn’t bother me.”.

But pouring herself into her work makes dealing with criticism a bit easier.

“I’m an entrepreneur at the end of the day,” she told TIME in an interview published April 30. “I want to expand in business, and I want to be able to do more things—but I’m definitely not in a rush.”.

A common osteoporosis drug blocked spinal damage in a surprising fresh study

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1477 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that an existing osteoporosis drug has shown surprising promise in protecting the spine from damage, raising hopes for upcoming treatments for chronic neck and back pain.
  • According to recent reports, the discovery could help scientists tackle one of the underlying causes of back pain: the gradual deterioration of the discs that cushion the bones of the spine.
  • Although the findings have not yet been confirmed in humans, they suggest that medications already used for other conditions could offer upcoming ways to slow spinal degeneration.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that an existing osteoporosis drug has shown surprising promise in protecting the spine from damage, raising hopes for upcoming treatments for chronic neck and back pain. In experiments involving zebrafish, researchers found that the medication prevented abnormal mineral deposits from forming in the spine, a process that can cause spinal tissues to harden and vertebrae to fuse together.

According to recent reports, the discovery could help scientists tackle one of the underlying causes of back pain: the gradual deterioration of the discs that cushion the bones of the spine. Researchers also identified changes in gene activity and metabolism that appear to contribute to this damage, revealing several possible targets for future treatments.

Although the findings have not yet been confirmed in humans, they suggest that medications already used for other conditions could offer upcoming ways to slow spinal degeneration. The research also demonstrates how zebrafish could help scientists investigate the causes of spinal disease and test potential therapies.

In a recent development, most people experience back pain at some point in their lives, and one common cause is the deterioration of the spine's natural shock absorbers. These structures, called intervertebral discs, sit between the vertebrae and help the spine absorb pressure, distribute weight, and move comfortably.

Recent findings suggest that over time, the discs can lose their ability to cushion the spine, a condition known as intervertebral disc degeneration (IVDD). As the discs deteriorate, they can contribute to pain, stiffness, and reduced mobility.

According to recent reports, despite the widespread impact and substantial economic burden of this condition, no medications are at the moment available that can stop or reverse the degenerative process. Surgery remains the only established long-term intervention for certain severe cases, creating an urgent need for treatments that address the underlying damage.

Researchers have long known that genetics influences the risk of developing spinal disc degeneration. One gene of particular interest is associated with collagen IX, a protein that helps maintain the structural integrity of spinal discs by supporting the network of fibers that holds them together. Variations affecting this gene have repeatedly been associated with disc problems that develop earlier in life.

To investigate how these genetic changes contribute to spinal damage, scientists at the Universities of Edinburgh and Bristol turned to zebrafish. They studied fish that had been bred without a functioning copy of the gene, allowing them to observe how its absence affected the spine as the animals grew older.

A Hidden Process Causes the Spine To Harden.

The results revealed striking similarities between the genetically altered zebrafish and people with degenerative spinal disease.

Recent findings suggest that as the fish aged, abnormal mineral deposits accumulated in the tissues separating their vertebrae. This process, known as mineralization, involves minerals collecting in tissues where they do not normally belong. In the spine, the buildup can cause normally flexible structures to become unusually rigid, much like unwanted bone forming in the wrong location.

Industry observers note that the researchers also observed spinal fusion, in which neighboring vertebrae become joined together. Such changes can interfere with the spine's normal flexibility and movement.

Importantly, the scientists discovered that the damage began well before the mineral deposits appeared. An underlying layer that provides structural support during spinal development started to break down first, suggesting that deterioration of this protective framework may set the stage for later hardening.

This finding could help explain how genetic changes initiate a chain reaction that eventually damages the spine.

Surprising Links to Fat Metabolism and Vitamin A.

According to recent reports, to understand what was happening at the molecular level, the team examined patterns of gene activity in the zebrafish. This allowed them to identify biological processes that had become unusually active or disrupted as spinal degeneration developed.

Several unexpected connections emerged.

The researchers found alterations in fat metabolism, the processes through which the body breaks down, stores, and uses fats. They also detected disturbances in a cellular signaling system called mTOR, which helps regulate cell growth, metabolism, and responses to nutrients.

Additional changes involved phosphate regulation and vitamin A signaling. Phosphate is an essential mineral involved in building bones and teeth, but its accumulation in the wrong tissues can contribute to abnormal hardening. Vitamin A signaling helps control how cells develop and function.

Together, these findings suggest that spinal disc degeneration involves more than the gradual wearing down of tissues. Changes in how cells process nutrients, regulate growth, and handle minerals may also play important roles.

An Osteoporosis Drug Blocks Spinal Mineral Buildup.

One of the most promising discoveries came when researchers tested ways to reduce the spinal abnormalities.

According to recent reports, A medication belonging to a class of drugs called bisphosphonates successfully blocked the abnormal mineral buildup in the zebrafish. Bisphosphonates are already used to treat osteoporosis, a condition in which bones become weaker and more vulnerable to fractures. These medications help protect bones by slowing the processes that break down bone tissue.

The finding is especially intriguing because it suggests that a treatment already used in patients might also help researchers develop therapies for spinal degeneration.

According to recent reports, the team identified other approaches that reduced spinal damage. Limiting how much food the zebrafish consumed led to fewer spinal fusions, as did medications that suppressed fat metabolism.

These results point toward fat metabolism and phosphate regulation as potentially crucial targets for future drugs.

However, the experiments were conducted in zebrafish, not humans. More research will be needed to determine whether the same biological mechanisms operate in people and whether targeting them can safely prevent or slow spinal disc degeneration. The dietary findings also do not establish that restricting food intake can prevent spinal damage in humans.

Fresh Hope for Chronic Back Pain Treatments.

The study was published in the journal Communications Biology and received support from Arthritis UK and BBSRC.

Dr. Erika Kague, who led the research at the University of Edinburgh's Institute of Genetics and Cancer, emphasized the potential significance of identifying treatments that target the underlying causes of spinal damage.

Industry observers note that "For decades, surgery has been the only real answer for disc disease. By understanding the biology that drives the spine to harden, our zebrafish studies point to several ways of slowing it down, including a drug already used safely in patients. There's more work to do, but for a condition that's affected people for generations without a treatment in sight, this is super exciting.".

The findings could be particularly crucial for the millions of people who live with persistent back pain and have limited options for preventing their condition from worsening.

Sources indicate that dr. Caroline Aylott, Head of Research Delivery at Arthritis UK, highlighted the potential benefits for patients.

"For the 9.5 million people across the UK living with back pain this research brings fresh hope that potential new therapeutic approaches are on the horizon.

"We are proud to fund research that is unlocking the science behind the processes leading to spinal disc degeneration. Back pain is one of the UK's most common conditions that has blighted millions over generations. Dr. Erika Kague and her team at the University of Edinburgh have uncovered important genetic evidence that could pave the way for new treatments, bringing us one step closer to a future where fewer people have to live with the daily pain and challenges that back pain can bring.".

The research also illustrates the broader value of studying basic biological processes to understand diseases that affect large numbers of people.

Dr. Jef Grainger, Executive Director for Bioscience Advancing Knowledge at BBSRC, remarked:.

"This research shows how publicly funded discovery bioscience can generate the knowledge needed to address major health challenges. By revealing upcoming knowledge of how healthy biological processes break down in aging-related spinal disc degeneration, the study opens up promising avenues for future treatment development. It's a great example of how BBSRC-supported research helps turn scientific discovery into knowledge and innovations that have the potential to improve people's lives.".

By identifying genetic and metabolic changes that contribute to spinal hardening, and demonstrating that some of the damage can be prevented in zebrafish, the researchers have opened several latest avenues for investigating spinal disc degeneration.

For a condition that affects millions and has no approved drug capable of stopping its progression, these early findings offer an encouraging starting point for developing treatments that could one day protect the spine before serious damage occurs.

Don Bluth on the future of animation and AI: Thats definitely a road I dont want to travel on

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1746 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mashable

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that for children of the '80s and '90s, Don Bluth was a major influence on how we saw the world.
  • Social media is evergreen with fans remembering the tender moments of Littlefoot and his tree star, or the terrifying ones, like Fievel or Mrs.
  • In a recent development, in an interview with Mashable, Bluth said watching the finished doc "brought tears to [his] eyes," because it refreshed memories of his colleagues.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that for children of the '80s and '90s, Don Bluth was a major influence on how we saw the world. With movies like The Secret of NIMH, An American Tail, The Land Before Time, All Dogs Go to Heaven, and Anastasia, this American animator offered us realms of adventure, with plucky heroes as well as villains so fantastically frightening that we carry the thrill of it all with us decades later.

Social media is evergreen with fans remembering the tender moments of Littlefoot and his tree star, or the terrifying ones, like Fievel or Mrs. Brisby being chased down by monstrous, roaring, ravenous cats. Now, for fans new and old, filmmakers Dave LaMattina and Chad N. Walker offer Don Bluth: Somewhere Out There, a documentary that explores the life and work of the innovative animator through his own words.

In a recent development, in an interview with Mashable, Bluth said watching the finished doc "brought tears to [his] eyes," because it refreshed memories of his colleagues. Together, they pursued animation not for the money but for the art and a deep desire to create something meaningful for future generations. Yet, when asked about his legacy, Bluth is quick to look back on the path that led him to his work.

He began by speaking of Winsor McCay, the father of American animation. In a wistful storyteller tone, Bluth recounted how a little boy witnessed the "magic" of the 1914 short film Gertie the Dinosaur, in which a pencil-sketched brontosaurus comes to life. This little boy was so inspired that he'd grow up to make his own animated short featuring a mouse named Mickey.

It has been revealed that that little boy, of course, was Walt Disney, who would go on to make 1937's Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs, the first animated feature film produced in the United States. That movie would go on to inspire a young Bluth, who'd direct his first animated feature in 1982 with The Secret of NIMH.

This path of inspiration to iconic art wasn't as direct a line as you might think.

Yes, Bluth scored a dream job, working at Disney Animation studio for 10 years on films like Sleeping Beauty, Robin Hood, and The Rescuers. But after Disney's death in 1966, Bluth and 17 other Disney animators feared the studio had lost their way, creatively.

Recent findings suggest that he told Mashable he'd invite these artists to his home on weekends, where they'd draw together to develop innovative pitches for their corporate bosses. When they were shot down, Bluth — along with Gary Goldman and John Pomeroy — built their own firm, Don Bluth Productions, to "see if we could do better than they were doing." For this, Bluth remembered, "We were called traitors.".

It has been revealed that that's not how Bluth saw his team. "[These] wonderful people had the courage to leave their jobs and security and go out there and try and do something great," he stated, "not just to feed their egos, but something they felt helped them grow up. And they wanted to give back.".

It was not an easy journey, as Don Bluth: Somewhere Out There details, revealing the highs and lows of Bluth's most beloved and worst-reviewed productions, as well as the wildly popular video game Dragon's Lair. In our interview, he spoke repeatedly about how the doc filled him with gratitude as he looked back for the filmmakers' interviews.

Industry observers note that to Mashable, he reflected, "What happened after so many movies, All Dogs Go to Heaven, American Tail, working with Steven Spielberg on both of those pictures, and George Lucas [on The Land Before Time], [it] became really, really obvious to us that we were doing the right thing [by] writing the right stories, and trying to make something that would move people's lives for the better — not just to pat our own backs and say, 'Look what we did.' [We were making] something that would help maybe children grow up and have some degree of morality about them. So then, that was our goal in everything.".

In Somewhere Out There, the rise of computer animation — which Bluth refers to as "3D animation" — came as a devastating blow to the animator, who'd spent his life developing the skills of hand-drawn 2D animation. To this day, Bluth still advocates for the artistry of hand-drawn animation.

"The way I look at this is animation in the 2D form is people, armed with a pencil in their hands, have to be able to draw," he explained, "and they also have to be able to act. And they have to have feelings about story.".

In a recent development, to Bluth, CGI movies aren't animation. "3D animation is puppetry," he remarked, adding, "[With 3D animation,] you drop your pencil. You put your hands on a keyboard, and you make a wireframe puppet act.".

It has been revealed that bluth shared several of his complaints about the look of 3D animation, saying, "To me, it looks very plastic... The colors are muted, and they're trying to put shading in there, trying to look more like a live-action picture." He asked, "Why are we trying to get to a place which looks more real?" adding, "That isn't the purpose at all of 2D [animation]. The purpose is to take you to a magical world. 2D is trying to make audiences come to our own world.".

Industry observers note that noting the animation industry changed forever with the massive success of 1995's Toy Story, Bluth noted, "Toy Story [movies] were quite fun to watch, but they didn't make me feel anything very deep. And animation is intended to do that, particularly with Walt Disney pictures. Snow White, Bambi, [and] Pinocchio — those pictures did something to change the way you thought and help you grow up in a way that was really good. And they did it in such a beautiful way.".

It was when Disney Studios, post-Walt, moved away from these tenets that Bluth and his colleagues set out on their own. He noted, "We left the Disney Studio because it was leaving out the morality statements and leaving out all the beautiful colors and everything.".

In terms of what recent animated films impressed Bluth, he stated, "I liked Klaus a lot," commending Sergio Pablos' inventive Christmas tale, which employs hand-drawn animation with a unique visual style.

Recent findings suggest that bluth also enjoyed Pete Docter's 2009 Pixar hit Up. "That was totally in 3D," he noted, "but it had a great story. For my taste, it went on too long. You know, the story was really about this couple promising each other they would go back to some place in their life, and she died. So, the man, true to the promise, tries to fulfill that [by taking their house on the journey]. So, I love that.".

Industry observers note that overall though, Bluth lamented, "Animation has become an advertisement for sugar cereal and whatever. There are more advertisements on animation than there are actually animated characters. The animated characters are just simply little puppets that jump up and down and tell one-line jokes. So, that's not good. Now, the last laugh is about to hit us like a tsunami; that is AI.".

According to recent reports, through the stories of Russian Jewish immigrant Fievel Mousekewitz, the widowed mother of four Mrs. Brisby, the orphaned brontosaurus Littlefoot, and rogue mutt Charlie B. Barkin, Bluth was striving to create stories that would inspire children to be good and creative, as Disney's movies had done for him. He doesn't see a future where AI can provide such mindful, moral guidance.

In a recent development, "It seems like AI is able to do wonderful, wonderful things," Bluth mused, "except AI is a machine, and it has no soul. It will borrow or steal, if you will, from everything that it knows, and give you what you ask for. But where's the creativity?".

"AI is a borrower," Bluth explained. "When you enter what you'd like to see, it searches all over and borrows it from other artists, puts it together. It highlights you on screen. Now, you can then make corrections. It can do all that, but it is still a machine. It doesn't ask you, 'Well, what is right and wrong? What is evil and good? What do you want me to say?' The machine can't do that.".

He continued, "The only thing you can do is go back to human beings and say, 'Don't replace human beings with machines.' They're the ones who have a heart, who have a soul, and probably have a Creator. So, there's a bigger picture that's going on than just animation on a screen.".

"AI has no soul," Bluth concluded. "It hasn't a clue how to write anything. Everything that you're going to see on your screen has been stolen from other artists.".

He allowed that some AI might be "stunningly beautiful," but "you'll find that it doesn't affect your heart the way you feel… They're not artists that are doing the AI. Many of them don't understand the art of acting or anything. So, what everything looks like in AI animation that I've seen, it all looks like slow motion, and it looks unreal. So, that's definitely a road I don't want to travel on.".

"I read somewhere where someone noted something that stuck in my head," he mused, paraphrasing Oscar Wilde's The Portrait of Dorian Gray. "There are many people who know the price of everything but the value of nothing. And I certainly hope that's not where we're going.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The first satellite in a constellation designed for humanitarian use will lift off next year, if all goes according to strategy.

The nonprofit Common Space plans to assemble a six-spacecraft constellation of Earth-observing satellites, whose high-resolution imagery will aid first responders, journalists, scientists and human-rights investigators around the world.

That strategy firmed up a bit today (Nov. 19), as Common Space revealed the builder of the first of those satellites: Satellogic, an Argentine-U.S. geospatial intelligence company.

There are more than 1,000 Earth-observing satellites circling our planet at the moment. But much of the data they gather is proprietary or too expensive to serve the common good, according to Common Space.

Recent findings suggest that the nonprofit wants to change that via its envisioned constellation, which it claims will collect imagery specifically for humanitarian and public-interest purposes. Common Space plans to operate on a "club-good model," which will share infrastructure and costs across a large community, allowing extensive, low-cost access to high-quality imagery.

Satellogic is now officially part of this picture.

"With Satellogic as our spacecraft partner, we're moving from vision to orbit and putting high-resolution data into the hands of those who need it most," Common Space co-founder Rhiannan Price said in a statement today. "This isn't just another satellite. We're building infrastructure to serve people for years to come.".

The satellite is Satellogic's NewSat Mark V, which Common Space selected after a competitive request-for-proposal process.

According to recent reports, the NewSat Mark V is just 32 inches (82 centimeters) long and weighs 85 pounds (38.5 kilograms) here on Earth. But the microsatellite packs a great deal of capability into that small package. From low Earth orbit (LEO), it naturally resolves features on the ground as small as 27.5 inches (70 cm), which Satellogic's proprietary algorithms can boost to a "super resolution" of 19.7 inches (50 cm).

Sources indicate that the satellite is scheduled to launch in July 2027, on a rocket that has yet to be unveiled. Satellogic will handle the preparations for that launch and manage satellite operations, which are expected to last at least five years in LEO. The manufacturer has extensive experience with such work; it has flown 61 of its Earth-observing satellites to date, all of which deployed successfully.

And Satellogic is aligned with Common Space philosophically, the organization stressed.

Sources indicate that "Common Space shares our belief that persistent global intelligence shouldn't be reserved for a few. Humanitarian responders and journalists are often first on the ground and last to get access, yet they need frequent, high-resolution imagery to see what's really happening so they can act with confidence," Luciano Giesso, vice president of space systems at Satellogic, said in the same statement. "This mission puts our vision of democratized access into practice.".

Sources indicate that common Space is currently raising money to expand the constellation to six satellites, which it hopes to have in place by 2030. This will allow daily high-resolution coverage of "priority areas," according to the nonprofit.

Sources indicate that editor's note: The original version of this story stated that the first Satellogic satellite will launch on a SpaceX rocket. This information was in an embargoed version of today's press release but was not in the final version, so it has been removed from this story.

  • Andoni Iraola indulged in his first fist-pumps towards the Kop after an utterly dominant, comfortable win illuminated by Rio Ngumoha and Florian Wirtz brilliance plus goals from Dominik Szoboszlai and Víctor Muñoz.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Green shoots of recovery have lasted longer in a blast furnace than in the Mauricio Pochettino era at Manchester United. On another abysmal Anfield day for the fallen giants of Manchester, Pochettino endured a baptism of fire from the eighth minute onwards when Leny Yoro was sent off for denying Alexander Isak a clear goalscoring opportunity. Liverpool would not be denied anything else while tormenting their old rivals yet again.

Andoni Iraola indulged in his first fist-pumps towards the Kop after an utterly dominant, comfortable win illuminated by Rio Ngumoha and Florian Wirtz brilliance plus goals from Dominik Szoboszlai and Víctor Muñoz. Liverpool’s two creative forces were also on the scoresheet as Ngumoha became the youngster scorer in the fixture’s Premier League history.

According to recent reports, “Poch is at the wheel” was the mocking, merciless soundtrack that accompanied the end of the former Tottenham, Chelsea and USA coach’s first traumatic game in the job. There may well be more. On this evidence, 19th in the Premier League is not a misleading reflection of United’s position.

The latest calamity in United’s worst start to a season for 40 years cannot be pinned on a head coach who met his new charges only on Wednesday. There can be no genuine takes on Pochettino’s vision for United either, given how swiftly he was forced to turn his first game into a damage-limitation exercise. But there was one firm conclusion to be drawn. His first massive call in the job proved a serious mistake with destructive repercussions for United’s entire evening.

Industry observers note that that ill-fated decision was to hand Matthijs de Ligt a first Premier League start in 12 months at the expense of Harry Maguire. Maguire may be a symbol of United’s inertia, but his replacement at centre-back was heavily responsible for the chaos that swiftly unfolded. The Netherlands international was at fault for three goals. Liverpool, under instruction from Iraola to start strong and “make them feel pressure from the beginning”, could hardly believe their luck at the first mishap in the visitors’ central defence.

In a recent development, • Accounting for 3pts/win all-time, Manchester United’s eight points this season are their fewest after 11 games of a league campaign since 1972-73 (7). That is also the previous season in which the Red Devils managed only one win through their first 11 league matches.

• Mauricio Pochettino (pictured) suffered the joint-heaviest defeat by a Manchester United manager in his first game (0-4), along with a defeat by the same scoreline for Lal Hilditch in October 1926 (0-4 v Bolton Wanderers in the top flight).

• Manchester United end the day in 19th position in the Premier League, with this the first time since November 1986 that they have been within the bottom two places of the league table having played at least 10 matches (21st in that case).

Recent findings suggest that • Mauricio Pochettino was the first manager in Premier League history to see his team concede twice and receive a red card in the first half of his first match in charge of a club. Opta.

De Ligt lost the flight of the ball and his man, Isak, when Ronald Araújo pinged a routine pass down Liverpool’s right-hand channel. Isak was suddenly away, De Ligt all at sea, and to compound matters Yoro was slow to react to the danger. By the time United’s covering defender was across to challenge Isak it was too late. Yoro clattered into the back of the Sweden international just outside the area and was shown a straight red card by the referee, Sam Barrott. Isak’s heavy first touch could not save Yoro. The free-kick could not save United from double jeopardy. Szoboszlai swept a powerful set piece into Senne Lammens’ bottom right-hand corner from 19 yards.

Sources indicate that pochettino claimed the dismissal was wrong and United should have had a penalty moments earlier for a Jérémy Jacquet challenge on Bryan Mbeumo. It was a desperate take. A simple detail showed the extent of the job United’s latest head coach has on his hands: the wall that lined up to face Szoboszlai’s free-kick. Just getting that right was beyond this group of players. White shirts lined up to protect the left side of Lammens’ goal but, with the isolated exception of Bruno Fernandes, no one covered the spot where the ball was ultimately placed.

According to recent reports, liverpool devoured the gifts. When the hosts doubled their lead three minutes later thoughts of another 7-0 humiliation for United did not seem unreasonable. Ngumoha tormented Diogo Dalot from the first whistle, as everyone inside the ground expected he would. Having been found by Isak’s cross-field pass the teenager breezed past Dalot to the byline and lifted a cross slightly behind Wirtz. The German playmaker, left in space by De Ligt, improvised brilliantly to hook a volley into the roof of the net while floating in mid-air. United were sinking into the abyss.

According to recent reports, the first chants of “sacked in the morning” flowed from the Kop towards a disbelieving United head coach. There were 14 minutes on the clock. It was, of course, a ludicrous chant. It might be months before United’s hapless owners are seeking another scapegoat.

According to recent reports, pochettino responded in the only way he could to the onslaught and introduced Maguire into a rejigged five-man defence. Whether in the knowledge that United possessed neither the ability nor the inclination to hurt them, Liverpool eased off for the remainder of the first half although Isak and Alexis Mac Allister could have extended the lead.

• Since the start of the 2021-22 season, Liverpool's four wins by 4+ goals against Manchester United are the most any Premier League team has achieved against another across all competitions.

Industry observers note that • Andoni Iraola is unbeaten in his seven Premier League matches against Manchester United (W3 D4). The only manager to record a longer unbeaten run against the Red Devils in the competition is Jürgen Klopp (8 between 2018 and 2022).

• This was the quickest Liverpool had gone 2-0 up in a Premier League match against Manchester United, going two ahead after just 12 minutes and 40 seconds.

• Rio Ngumoha (18y 85d) became the youngest player to score and assist in a Premier League game for Liverpool since Michael Owen on Boxing Day 1997 (18y 12d v Leeds United).

• Dominik Szoboszlai (pictured) scored his fifth direct free kick for Liverpool in the Premier League; only Jamie Redknapp (8), Steven Gerrard (7) and Trent Alexander-Arnold (6) have netted more for the club in the competition.

• Florian Wirtz created 10 chances in open play for Liverpool, the most by a player in a Premier League match since Manchester City’s David Silva against West Brom in March 2015 (11). Opta.

Liverpool did not let their rivals off so lightly after the restart. Bradley Barcola could and should have provided Wirtz with a hat-trick of assists but squandered three beautiful touches from his fellow £100m+ recruit. Virgil van Dijk put a free header wide from another fine delivery by Wirtz. Barcola turned provider in devastating style, however, to create the goal Ngumoha’s display richly deserved. The France winger burst away from Lisandro Martínez and Fernandes with one flick of the ball before delivering an assist on a plate for the teenager to convert.

In a recent development, iraola’s thoughts started to drift towards the midweek Champions League trip to Club Brugge and he started resting players from the 72nd minute onwards. But Liverpool were not done. Another mistake by De Ligt, this time a sloppy pass infield, was pounced on by Wirtz who released Muñoz inside the box. The Liverpool substitute stroked an emphatic finish past Lammens. All Sir Alex Ferguson could do up in the directors’ box in the closing stages was laugh with his friend the actor James Nesbit. The alternative is too bleak for a proud United man to contemplate.

Champion’s corner: KC Current win first NWSL Championship with 2-1 stunner over Spirit

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1007 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Debinha, Trinity Rodman trade goals in stoppage time.
  • Washington Spirit lose third consecutive NWSL final.
  • It took five years, 90 minutes and a goal for the ages, but the Kansas City Current have their first-ever NWSL championship.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Current’s opener came direct from a corner kick.

Debinha, Trinity Rodman trade goals in stoppage time.

Washington Spirit lose third consecutive NWSL final.

Read Jeff Rueter’s minute-by-minute report.

It took five years, 90 minutes and a goal for the ages, but the Kansas City Current have their first-ever NWSL championship.

Riding a wave of momentum created by a 54th-minute Olimpico from midfielder Vanessa DiBernardo, and capping it off with an all-crucial breakaway winner from Debinha, the Current silenced the partisan, sellout crowd at the heavily-favored Washington Spirit’s home ground with a 2-1 victory on Saturday.

The Spirit, heartbroken at the final whistle, have now lost three consecutive NWSL Championships.

Recent findings suggest that “Obviously this one hurts way worse than any of the other ones,” forward Trinity Rodman remarked afterward. “I don’t even think you have words in this moment — it is too fresh.”.

DiBernardo’s goal was stunning, a driven, bent corner kick played to the far post that eluded Spirit goalkeeper Sandy MacIver, her defenders and Current forward Haley Hopkins, potentially DiBernardo’s intended target. The Spirit’s players and fans alike pleaded with center referee Joshua Encarnación, suggesting he examine the play on VAR for obstruction, as MacIver had potentially been screened. The review never came.

Sources indicate that whether played directly on goal intentionally or otherwise, the effort will go down as one of the most memorable in NWSL Championship history. At 34, DiBernardo becomes the oldest player in league history to score in a final, and was later named the match’s MVP.

According to recent reports, “I’ve been to the game a few times and haven’t won, but this one just felt a little lighter,” noted DiBernardo, who gave birth to Charlie, her first child, in January and took time off before returning to the Current in March. “I think just having Charlie, it just brings a different perspective on life. I knew the game was massive and it was a big moment, but just kinda having her, just spending the day with her, it just felt really special.”.

The game’s early phases were forgettable save for one incident which would go on to affect the remainder of the match: a bruising, high-speed tackle on Rodman by Current defender Laney Rouse in the fifth minute. The challenge sent Rodman flying and appeared to injure her left elbow; the Spirit forward, nearing tears, spent much of the first half in visible pain and seemingly never fully recovered. Rouse was not cautioned for the challenge.

It has been revealed that “[It helped set the tone] in the sense that it hurt really bad, yes,” Rodman said. “As a team, you always want to put the first hit in. You’re taught to do that. Credit to them. I wish I was the one who put her on the ground. They did a really good job at setting the tone and controlling the first half.”.

According to recent reports, it was far from the game’s only physical moment. Neither team managed to settle into any meaningful rhythm during an opening 45 that felt at times more like a title fight than a title match. Encarnación, involved in his first NWSL final, called a very tight match and the near-constant stoppages in play were the defining characteristic of a sometimes ugly opening phase. In many ways it was not entirely his fault: the message-sending start from KC and the Spirit’s subsequent response often compelled him to act. The 19 combined first-half fouls between both sides were the most in any half of any NWSL title match in league history.

Industry observers note that “It felt like we couldn’t play more than two minutes without a whistle,” Rodman said. “We were fouling, they were true calls for sure — but I think you lose control of the game really quickly that way ... It definitely messed with our rhythm a little bit.”.

Paradoxically, though, the match was won with speed. Deep into second-half stoppage time, the Current found their eventual match-winner on a breakaway. After doggedly winning back possession after a Spirit free kick late on, Kansas City forward Debinha streaked upfield from just beyond the center stripe, looking off a wide-open Temwa Chawinga and rounding MacIver who looked on hopelessly as the Brazilian slotted it home.

It has been revealed that moments later, Rodman – somehow still in the match after not only the early challenge but a later high-speed collision with Current goalkeeper Lorena – pulled one back for the Spirit. Falling away from goal 10 yards out, Rodman got her head on the end of a Tara Rudd cross, placing it perfectly over Lorena’s outstretched arms and into the far-side netting. The ensuing five minutes – the game ended in the 102nd – were chaotic but the Spirit couldn’t quite find the equalizer.

According to recent reports, after a slow start, the Current were well-managed by former Major League Soccer and US national team member Chris Armas. Armas was widely considered a controversial selection at the time of his appointment but proceeded to lead the club to their first championship in his first season, doing so by beating Gotham FC and now the Spirit, two sides picked by many as potential league-winners.

“I think from the front to the back we made it a point that every person on this team defends and if somebody is going to make a mistake the other person is going to have their back,” Current defender Izzy Rodriguez stated. “We try and turn every 1v1 situation into a 1v2 for us, and I think that showed up today. We were winning our duels and second balls and those are things that win games.”.

For the Spirit, the loss is devastating. They become the first American professional club – men’s or women’s – to lose three consecutive finals since the Upcoming England Revolution of Major League Soccer, who did so in the mid 2000s. In their five Championship appearances, the Spirit have won just one time, in 2021.
